# Connect

## Connect Security

<sub>`Connect-Security.ps1`</sub>

Connects this console to Security and Compliance (IPPSSession).

This is the endpoint behind content search, eDiscovery, retention labels and
DLP policies.

The console closes, the sign-in happens, and the console reopens with the
connection live. That is deliberate -- a sign-in window cannot accept typing
while the console's own window is in front of it.

IT IS NOT THE SAME AS EXCHANGE ONLINE, even though both come from the
ExchangeOnlineManagement module and both may use the same account. They are
separate sessions to separate endpoints, and the header reports them
separately. Being connected to ExO tells you nothing about this one.

BOTH SESSIONS IN ONE PROCESS SHARE CMDLET NAMES. Where a name exists in both
endpoints, the one that answers is whichever module state won last. If a
compliance cmdlet starts returning Exchange-shaped results, that is why --
reconnect this session.

## Connect Teams

<sub>`Connect-Teams.ps1`</sub>

Connects this console to Microsoft Teams.

IT USES DEVICE SIGN-IN. No window pops up. A code and a URL are printed in
the console window -- open the URL anywhere, type the code, and this finishes
on its own. If you are waiting for a prompt to appear you are waiting for
something that is not coming; read the code instead.

The console closes first so there IS a console to print the code into, then
reopens with the connection live.

ONLY THE TEAMS TOOLS NEED THIS. The Exchange, SharePoint and AD tools do not
use it and are not greyed when it is absent.

CONNECTING TO TEAMS DOES NOT CONNECT YOU TO ANYTHING ELSE. It is a separate
sign-in from Exchange Online even when it is the same account, and the header
reports the two independently.

## Console

<sub>`console.ps1` &nbsp;|&nbsp; Tier 3 &nbsp;|&nbsp; works on: Mailbox</sub>

A PowerShell prompt that shares the console's live connections.

For the times a tool does not cover what you need and you want to run cmdlets
by hand, without connecting to everything again in a new window.

Whatever the console is connected to, this is connected to. That includes the
ability to change things, with none of the previews or confirmations the tools
give you.

## Dashboard

<sub>`Dashboard.ps1`</sub>

**Runs against:** nothing new. It reads what the console already knows and

The start-of-day page. Six panels answering the questions worth asking before
you touch anything:

  ENVIRONMENT      Am I connected to what I need, and is PIM still active?
  TOOLKIT HEALTH   Is my copy complete and current?
  TODAY            What has run today, and did any of it fail?
  RETRY QUEUE      Is anything sitting unfinished from a disable run?
  TOP TOOLS        What actually gets used.
  FAILURE HOTSPOTS What keeps going wrong, so it can be fixed.

READ-ONLY. Nothing here changes a mailbox, a group or a file. The buttons
open other tools; they do not act.

The connection and version panels call the SAME functions as the console
header and footer rather than working it out again -- so the two cannot
disagree with each other. A second opinion about your own state is worse
than one.

ABOUT "UNKNOWN" RESULTS: rows converted from the old two-column log have no
Result, because that log never recorded one. They are counted as Unknown, not
folded into Success. The count shrinks on its own as those rows age out.

## ExO

<sub>`Connect-ExO.ps1`</sub>

Connects this console to Exchange Online.

The console closes, the sign-in happens, and the console reopens with the
connection live. That is deliberate -- a sign-in window cannot accept typing
while the console's own window is open in front of it, so the console gets out
of the way.

Complete the sign-in and MFA prompt when it appears; the console comes back on
its own.

## Forget API Credentials

<sub>`Forget-ApiCredentials.ps1`</sub>

**Runs against:** NOTHING. Clears in-memory credentials. No system is contacted.

Forget the API credentials held in memory for this session.

Proofpoint, SER and SendGrid credentials are asked for once per session and
kept in memory. This clears them. The next tool that needs one asks again.

IT ALSO CLEARS ANY CACHED BEARER TOKEN. A token minted from a cleared client
secret is still a live credential -- forgetting the secret and leaving the
token would make the promise false.

NOTHING WAS EVER ON DISK, so there is nothing to clean up anywhere else. This
only affects the running console and the tools it launches.

## OnPrem

<sub>`Connect-ExSE.ps1`</sub>

Connects this console to on-premises Exchange.

Uses your current Windows sign-in -- no password prompt -- by importing a
session from the hybrid server.

Needed by anything that touches the on-premises directory: distribution list
management, new starters, terminations and the on-premises reports.

## SPO

<sub>`Connect-SPO.ps1`</sub>

Connects this console to SharePoint Online.

Same pattern as the Exchange Online button: the console closes, you sign in,
and it reopens with the connection live.

Needed by the OneDrive and SharePoint reports. The Exchange tools do not use
it.

## Set PIM Timer

<sub>`Set-PimTimer.ps1`</sub>

**Runs against:** nothing against the tenant. Writes one timestamp to your local profile.

Starts the PIM countdown in the console header, without opening the portal.

The jump box cannot reach the PIM activation portal, so activation happens
elsewhere. This button is the "I have activated" note: press it once your
access is active and the header starts counting down from the tenant's
activation length (Pim.DurationHours in Tenant.json -- 9 hours here),
going amber under 30 minutes and red when it runs out.

It is a NOTE, not a live reading. Entra is not consulted. If a countdown is
already running you are asked before it is reset, so a second click does
not quietly hand you nine hours you do not have.

Press it again after re-activating. Nothing else to configure.

# Daily Scripts

## AD Lookup

<sub>`AD-Lookup.ps1`</sub>

**Runs against:** On-premises Exchange and Active Directory. Reads only, unless you edit an attribute.

Type part of a name. Get back every matching object, with what it IS and
where it lives.

Built for the moment a ticket says "give Send As on the ABCD-Shared mailbox"
and you have no idea what the address is, or whether it is a mailbox at all.
Search ABCD, read the Type column, double-click the right row, and the address
is on your clipboard ready to paste into the tool that does the work.

THE TYPE COLUMN IS THE POINT. These all look alike in a name list and behave
nothing alike:

  UserMailbox / SharedMailbox      Full Access and Send As both work
  MailUniversalDistributionGroup   Send As works, Full Access is meaningless
  MailUniversalSecurityGroup       a distribution list that also grants rights
  MailContact                      no mailbox anywhere; nothing to delegate
  RemoteSharedMailbox              the mailbox is in the cloud; the object here
                                   is the on-premises stub that syncs it

Getting this wrong is not a typo, it is twenty minutes and a confused reply.

THE OU COLUMN answers the other half of the question -- which office or
business unit owns this, and which directory it came from.

ATTRIBUTES opens the selected object in an editor. Everything populated is
shown; 46 attributes are editable -- names, job and organisation, every phone
field, the full address, and all fifteen extensionAttributes.

WHAT IS READ-ONLY, AND WHY IT IS A SHORT LIST:
  addresses      mail and proxyAddresses belong to Exchange. Editing them
                 behind its back is how an object gets two primaries.
  identity       sAMAccountName, userPrincipalName, cn, name. Changing one of
                 these is a migration, not an edit.
  relationships  member, memberOf, managedBy, manager -- the value is a
                 distinguished name, and a text box invites somebody to type
                 a person's name into it.
  state          userAccountControl and the timestamps. Enabling an account by
                 hand-editing a bitmask is a way to be wrong quietly.
  anything with more than one value, which is shown as 'multi (n)'. Writing
  one value back would silently discard the rest.

IT WORKS ON GROUPS, which the old All Attributes tools did not: they used
Get-ADUser and simply failed on anything that was not a user. Half of what
this finds is a distribution list.

'Also search Active Directory' adds objects with NO mailbox -- the plain
security group sitting next to the shared mailbox with almost the same name.
It cannot be delegated to, but seeing it explains why the name looked
ambiguous. Off by default because it is slower.

Reading is safe. The only thing that writes is the attribute editor, and it
confirms every change and records it in the audit log.

## Blocked Senders

<sub>`BlockedSenders.ps1`</sub>

Shows every account the service has blocked from sending mail, and lets you
release one.

An account lands here after sending mail the service classified as spam. In
practice that is usually a deliberate bulk send that went out the wrong way
-- but it is ALSO what a compromised mailbox looks like, and the two are
indistinguishable from this list alone. Find out which before releasing.

WHAT YOU SEE BEFORE YOU ACT:

  Reason         why the service blocked them, in its own words
  Blocked        when it happened
  Released here  how many times this toolkit has released this address
                 before, and when it last did

That last column is worth reading. A second release is a coincidence; a
fourth is a pattern, and the pattern is usually a team that keeps forgetting
the bulk-send tool. Releasing them again fixes today and not next week.

MICROSOFT LIMITS HOW MANY TIMES AN ACCOUNT CAN BE RELEASED. Exceed it and the
release fails and only a support case will clear it -- so the count is not
only a habit tracker, it is a budget.

The ticket reference you type is recorded with the release, in the audit log
AND in the service, so "who released this and why" is answerable later.

Releasing does not fix the cause. If the account was compromised, releasing
it hands the mailbox back to whoever took it.

## Header Analyzer

<sub>`HeaderAnalyzer.ps1`</sub>

Paste the raw internet headers from an email and get a readable summary of
what happened to it.

  * the delivery path, oldest hop first, with how long each hop took
  * SPF, DKIM and DMARC results, and Microsoft's composite verdict
  * the Exchange Online filtering result -- spam confidence, bulk level,
    and WHY it was filtered, in words rather than codes
  * anything worth a second look, like a Reply-To that points somewhere
    other than the From address

Useful for "why did this go to junk", "why was this blocked", and "is this
actually from who it says it is".

Everything happens on this machine. Nothing is uploaded, which is the main
reason it exists -- headers contain internal server names, addresses and
subject lines that should not be pasted into a public website.

To get the headers: in Outlook, open the message, File > Properties, and
copy the Internet headers box.

## Inbox Rules

<sub>`InboxRules.ps1` &nbsp;|&nbsp; Tier 1 &nbsp;|&nbsp; works on: Mailbox</sub>

**Runs against:** reads the mailbox's inbox rules. Enable, Disable and Delete change them and ask first.

View, disable, enable and delete the inbox rules on someone's mailbox.

The usual reasons to look: mail vanishing into a folder nobody remembers
creating, mail being forwarded somewhere it should not be, or a rule left
behind by a compromise. The RISK column does that first read for you:

  EXTERNAL FORWARD   forwards, redirects or forwards-as-attachment to an
                     address outside the accepted domains. The classic
                     compromise rule. Red.
  DELETES            deletes the message, or moves it to Deleted Items,
                     Junk, RSS or Conversation History -- the folders
                     nobody looks in. Red.
  HIDES              marks as read and stops processing, with no visible
                     effect -- the quiet half of a compromise. Amber.
  forward (internal) forwards to somebody in the company. Plain.

Tick the rules you want and press Enable / Disable / Delete. Delete cannot
be undone; Disable can, so prefer it while you are still working out
whether a rule is wanted. Click a row to read its full description in the
pane below.

'Include hidden' also lists the rules Outlook and other clients create for
themselves -- they are normally noise, but a compromise can hide there too.

Export writes the grid to the reports folder as <mailbox>_InboxRules.csv.

Exchange Online only.

## Mailbox Health

<sub>`MailboxHealth.ps1` &nbsp;|&nbsp; Tier 1 &nbsp;|&nbsp; works on: Mailbox</sub>

A read-only snapshot of one mailbox -- the first place to look when someone
says "my email is doing something strange".

Shows size and quota, the mailbox type, forwarding, delegates and
permissions, auto-reply state, and the litigation hold and archive status
in one view, so you are not running six commands to answer one question.

Read-only. Nothing here changes anything -- it is for finding out what is
true before you decide what to do.

## Manage Mail Object

<sub>`ManageMailObject.ps1`</sub>

Creates and removes shared mailboxes and distribution groups on-premises.

Type the address -- with or without the domain -- pick the object type, pick
Add or Remove, then Preview and Apply.

ON ADD it needs a directory, because that decides which OU the object lands
in. Directories that have an OU configured in Tenant Manager use it without
asking; ones that do not will ask you for the OU.

Shared mailboxes are created as REMOTE mailboxes -- the AD account is created
on-premises and the mailbox itself lives in the cloud. That is what makes them
appear after a sync cycle rather than immediately.

ON REMOVE it needs nothing but the address, but it will not act on what it has
not identified. It looks the object up, shows you what it found, and refuses
if the object is not the type you selected. Typing a person's address into
Remove Shared Mailbox would otherwise delete their mailbox.

  Remove   deletes the AD account. The cloud mailbox is soft-deleted and
           recoverable for a limited window.
  Disable  keeps the AD account and strips its mail attributes.
Disable is the reversible one and is offered as a checkbox on Remove.

Owner is optional. On a shared mailbox it grants FullAccess and SendAs; on a
distribution group it sets ManagedBy, which also lets that person edit the
membership from Outlook.

Distribution groups reject external senders unless you tick the box.

## Message Trace

<sub>`MessageTrace.ps1` &nbsp;|&nbsp; Tier 1 &nbsp;|&nbsp; works on: Mailbox</sub>

Follow a message through Exchange Online -- where it went, whether it was
delivered, and what happened if it was not.

Search by sender, recipient, subject and date range, and filter by status so
you can show only failures or only quarantined items. Results can be filtered
further with the search box without re-running the trace.

Quarantined messages can be released from here.

DOUBLE-CLICK A RESULT for the full event timeline of that one message --
every hop, and any TRANSPORT RULES that acted on it, named. Rule hits are
listed at the top of the pane and marked with >> in the timeline.

That answers "why did this get redirected / stamped / blocked", which the
result grid alone cannot: the grid shows the outcome, the detail shows the
cause. Transport Rules then shows that rule's priority and what it sets --
priority being what decides which of several matching rules won.

Microsoft only keeps trace data for a limited window -- roughly the last ten
days for the detailed view. For anything older you need a historical search,
which Microsoft runs as a background job.

WHEN THIS IS THE WRONG TOOL

Message trace answers "what happened to this message" -- where it went, and
why it did not arrive. It does not do threat hunting.

For URL and attachment verdicts, campaign views, saved queries or bulk
remediation, use THREAT EXPLORER instead. The button at the bottom opens it
in your admin browser profile. It needs Defender for Office 365 Plan 2.

Threat Explorer does not open carrying your filter. Select a row here, use
Copy Sender or Copy Message-ID, and paste that into the portal's own filter.

Read-only apart from releasing quarantine.

## Out of Office

<sub>`OOFEditor.ps1` &nbsp;|&nbsp; Tier 2 &nbsp;|&nbsp; works on: Mailbox</sub>

**Runs against:** reads the auto-reply configuration. Save changes it and asks first.

Read and set someone's out-of-office message without needing their mailbox
open. Both messages -- internal, and the one external senders receive --
and the state, audience and schedule.

THE EDITOR IS A REAL ONE. Exchange stores auto-reply text as HTML, so the
message boxes are HTML editors, not plain text: font, size, colour,
highlight, bold/italic/underline, bullets, alignment, links -- the same
things a person would do in Outlook. Ctrl+B / Ctrl+I / Ctrl+U work. What
you see is what the sender gets.

TEMPLATES. Three standard messages (back on a date, extended leave, left
the company). Pick one, press Insert, fill in the two or three blanks --
return date comes from the End picker if it is set, the name from the
mailbox -- and edit from there. A template REPLACES the tab you are on,
and asks first if there is something in it.

PREVIEW shows each message exactly as it will render, with the HTML
source alongside for the times something looks wrong and you need to see
why. Copy -> External copies the internal message over the external one.

Scheduled needs both a start and an end; the pickers are only live in that
state. External audience: None (external senders get nothing), Known
(contacts only), All.

Exchange Online only.

## Quarantine Manager

<sub>`QuarantineManager.ps1` &nbsp;|&nbsp; Tier 2 &nbsp;|&nbsp; works on: Mailbox</sub>

**Runs against:** Exchange Online quarantine. Reads only, until you press Release or Delete.

Searches the Exchange Online quarantine by recipient, sender, subject, age
and quarantine type, and lists what it finds in a grid.

From the grid you can:
  Preview headers          read the message header without releasing it
  Release to recipient     deliver to every ORIGINAL recipient (-ReleaseToAll)
  Release + Report FP      the same, and tell Microsoft it was a false positive
                           (the service only accepts the report for Spam)
  Delete                   remove from quarantine (soft delete, not -HardDelete)
  Export CSV               write the current grid to the reports folder

Every release and delete shows the exact list first and asks. Each row is
acted on separately, so one failure does not stop the rest, and every
success and failure is written to the audit log.

The search reads at most 30 days back (the service keeps no more) and stops
at 1000 results; the summary says so when that cap is hit. It never
releases to an address that was not an original recipient, and never
hard-deletes.

## Quick Links

<sub>`QuickLaunch.ps1`</sub>

Your own set of links, as buttons.

Each link opens in the Edge profile it was set up with, so admin portals open
with the elevated account and everyday links do not. Links marked as admin are
dark blue, so you can see which is which before you click.

Type in the Find box to narrow a long list.

Edit the links, their order and their sections in QuickLaunch Tool.

Opens links in a browser. Connects to nothing.

## Retention Policy

<sub>`Retention-Policy.ps1`</sub>

**Runs against:** Reads CustomAttribute8 from a mailbox. Read-only.

Which retention policy a mailbox is on.

Type any of these and press Check:
  the alias            jsmith
  the first part       john.smith
  the whole address    john.smith@contoso.com

THE ANSWER COMES FROM CustomAttribute8. An empty attribute is not missing
data -- it means the mailbox is on the standard policy, which is why a blank
reads as "Default 3 Year Retention Policy" rather than as an error.

THAT DISTINCTION MATTERS BOTH WAYS. A blank attribute and a mailbox that does
not exist are completely different answers, and this tool never reports one as
the other: a mailbox it cannot find is reported as not found, never as the
default policy.

IT IS A LABEL, NOT AN ENFORCED SETTING. CustomAttribute8 is free text that
something else acts on. This tool reports what is written there; it does not
prove any policy is actually applied to the mailbox.

Read-only. It reports and changes nothing.

## Search and Purge

<sub>`Search_Purge.ps1`</sub>

**Runs against:** Reads Content Search results from the Security and Compliance session, and DELETES mail when told to. Writes CSVs.

Find content across mailboxes and Teams, look at what was found, and delete
it -- all of it, or only the rows you tick.

IT NEEDS THE SECURITY AND COMPLIANCE SESSION, not Exchange Online. They are
different endpoints that share cmdlet names. If the Security indicator in the
console is red, press Connect-IPPSSession first; this window will refuse until
it is green, and say so rather than failing halfway through a purge.

THE THREE TABS ARE A SEQUENCE:

  1. Create a search   -- what to look for and where.
  2. Searches          -- run one, watch its status, delete one.
  3. Preview and purge -- see the items, tick some, delete.

TO FIND EVERYTHING FROM ONE PERSON, put their address in "From (sender)". It
becomes from:"..." in the query, which is shown in full above the button
before anything runs -- READ IT. If the sender is not in that query, the
search is not filtered by sender, however many items it returns.

"Custom start / end" ARE DATES AND NOTHING ELSE. They are greyed out unless
Date range is "Custom range", because they were once labelled "From / To" and
an address typed into them was accepted and silently discarded: the search
then returned every message in the mailbox and looked broken. For cc and bcc
as well as To, use participants:"..." in the Keywords box.

ABOUT DELETING, AND PLEASE READ THIS ONCE:

"Purge everything this search found" is the operation Microsoft actually
provides. It deletes the whole result set.

"Purge only the ticked rows" is NOT an operation Microsoft provides. This tool
fakes it honestly: it builds a second search narrowed to the rows you ticked,
runs it, and compares the count. If that narrowed search matches MORE items
than you ticked -- which happens when a subject is not unique -- IT REFUSES,
because the alternative is deleting somebody else's mail as well. Narrow the
original search instead and try again.

THE PREVIEW LIST IS NOT ALWAYS THE WHOLE RESULT SET. Microsoft caps preview at
roughly a thousand items. The window always tells you the previewed count and
the search's own count, and warns when they differ -- if they do, "purge
everything" will delete far more than the list in front of you shows.

A SINGLE PURGE DOES NOT NECESSARILY FINISH THE JOB. Microsoft limits how many
items one purge action removes per mailbox. Re-run it, and check the count
each time, until the search returns nothing.

Soft delete puts items in Recoverable Items, where a user can get them back
for the retention window. Hard delete does not. Nothing here recovers them.

## Spam Policy Viewer

<sub>`SpamPolicyViewer.ps1` &nbsp;|&nbsp; Tier 1 &nbsp;|&nbsp; works on: Mailbox</sub>

**Runs against:** reads anti-spam, anti-phish and outbound spam policies and rules from Exchange Online. Changes nothing.

Answers "which spam policy applies to this mailbox, and what does it do?"

"Why did this get through" and "why was this blocked" are unanswerable
until you know which policy won. Exchange picks the policy the same way
for anti-spam, anti-phish and outbound spam: rules are walked in Priority
order (0 first), the first ENABLED rule whose conditions match the
recipient and whose exceptions do not wins, and if nothing matches the
Default policy applies.

This tool walks that ladder for one address and shows the winning policy,
the rule that selected it, WHY it matched, the settings that matter, and
the whole ladder so you can see what would have won instead.

Group-scoped rules (SentToMemberOf / FromMemberOf) are flagged as
"possibly" -- membership is NOT expanded. Check the group yourself.

Read-only. Writes a CSV of the effective settings only when you ask.

## Unblock Files

<sub>`UnBlock.ps1`</sub>

**Runs against:** nothing. It only touches files already on this machine.

Clears the mark-of-the-web from every file in the toolkit folder.

WHAT IT IS FOR. A file that arrived by download, email or a copy from another
machine carries a flag saying so. PowerShell then refuses to dot-source it,
or warns on every launch -- which on a toolkit of a hundred scripts means a
hundred warnings, or a console that will not start.

RUN IT ONCE after copying a new build in. Nothing else needs doing.

IT WORKS ON THE FOLDER IT IS IN, found from its own location -- so it cannot
unblock the wrong copy of the toolkit, which is what the previous version
did when it was pointed at one hardcoded path.

READ-ONLY as far as any mailbox, group or directory is concerned. It changes
a file attribute and nothing else.

## Unified Lookup

<sub>`Unified-Lookup.ps1`</sub>

**Runs against:** On-premises Exchange, Active Directory and Exchange Online. Reads everywhere; writes only the one attribute you confirm.

Type part of a name. Get back everything that matches, from everywhere.

FOUR SOURCES, SEARCHED TOGETHER:

  On-premises AD         ALWAYS. Distribution lists, mail-enabled security
                         groups, shared / room / equipment mailboxes, remote
                         mailbox stubs, mail contacts -- read straight from
                         Active Directory, which needs no Exchange connection
                         of any kind. Tick the box to add objects with no
                         address at all (plain security groups).
  On-premises Exchange   when the Exchange Management Shell is loaded. Adds
                         Exchange's own recipient type, which knows about
                         room lists and arbitration mailboxes that no AD
                         attribute distinguishes.
  Exchange Online        cloud distribution lists, Microsoft 365 groups,
                         shared / room mailboxes, contacts, room lists
  Soft-deleted           mailboxes deleted in the cloud but still recoverable

CONNECTIONS ARE THE CONSOLE'S JOB, NOT THIS TOOL'S. This runs in the console's
own process, so whatever the console is connected to, this is connected to. If
the line at the top says Exchange Online is missing, use Connect ExO in the
console and search again -- no need to close this window.

THE SOURCE COLUMN IS THE ANSWER TO A QUESTION YOU ASK CONSTANTLY:

  On-prem        exists only on-premises -- not synced, or not yet
  Cloud          created in the cloud; there is no on-premises object at all
  Synced         found in BOTH. The on-premises object is the authority and
                 the cloud copy follows it. Editing the cloud side directly
                 is the change that silently reverts on the next sync.
  Soft-deleted   deleted, still recoverable, still holding its address

ONE ROW PER OBJECT. A synced object is found twice and shown once, merged on
its primary address, because two rows for one thing is not an answer -- it is
the raw material of one.

WHAT IT DOES NOT SEARCH: Entra security groups that are not mail-enabled. No
Exchange cmdlet returns them and Graph is not available here yet. A cloud-only
security group will not appear -- that is a gap, not a result.

THIS TOOL WRITES. It did not used to, and the difference matters.

  Attributes   WHAT THE OBJECT IS -- display name, alias, primary address,
               hide-from-GAL, the fifteen custom attributes. For a cloud-only
               object it edits here, with Set-Mailbox / Set-DistributionGroup /
               Set-MailContact / Set-MailUser / Set-UnifiedGroup as the type
               requires. For anything with a distinguished name it opens
               AD-Lookup, because Active Directory is the authority.
  Mailbox      HOW THE MAILBOX BEHAVES -- forwarding, and whether sending as
               settings     the mailbox leaves a copy in ITS Sent Items.
               Always Exchange Online, because that is where a mailbox lives.
  Open         WHAT THE OBJECT DOES -- a group opens its membership, a mailbox
               opens its permissions.

WHY ATTRIBUTES AND MAILBOX SETTINGS ARE TWO BUTTONS. A RemoteSharedMailbox has
its directory object on-premises and its MAILBOX in Exchange Online. One row,
two homes. Folding both into one button left one of them unreachable -- and it
did: send-as copies could not be set on any synced shared mailbox at all.

THE SOURCE COLUMN DECIDES WHICH SIDE IS WRITTEN, and that is the safety
property worth having in one tool. A SYNCED object is edited ON-PREMISES,
always -- Active Directory is the authority and a cloud-side change to a
synced object reverts on the next sync cycle. Nothing else in the toolkit
stops you making that mistake in another window.

Every change is confirmed before it is written and recorded in the audit log.

## new OOF

<sub>`new-OOF.ps1`</sub>

**Runs against:** Exchange Online

Reads and sets automatic replies on a mailbox.

# Mailbox and Access

## All Attributes

<sub>`AllAttributes.ps1` &nbsp;|&nbsp; Tier 3 &nbsp;|&nbsp; works on: Mailbox</sub>

A wider view of the directory attributes on an account, beyond the mail ones.

Use it when something is set that should not be, or missing when it should be
there, and you need to see the raw value rather than what a UI reports.

Editing here writes directly to the attribute with no validation beyond what
the directory itself enforces. Read Mail Attributes first if the field is a
mail one -- it understands addresses properly.

## Automap Fix

<sub>`Automap-Fix.ps1`</sub>

**Runs against:** WRITES mailbox permissions in Exchange Online. Removes and re-adds Full Access.

Fix a shared mailbox that will not appear in somebody's Outlook.

It removes their Full Access, waits, and adds it back. That is the fix,
because AUTOMAPPING IS DECIDED WHEN THE PERMISSION IS GRANTED and never
revisited -- if it did not take the first time, nothing will change it except
granting it again.

THIS BRIEFLY REMOVES THEIR ACCESS. For about ten seconds they have none. If
they are working in the mailbox right now, do it later.

IT IS NOT INSTANT AFTERWARDS. Outlook picks up the new mapping when it next
reconnects -- usually minutes, sometimes at the next restart. A user watching
their Outlook while you press the button will see nothing happen and conclude
it failed. Tell them to close and reopen Outlook.

AUTOMAPPING ONLY WORKS WHEN THE PERMISSION IS ON THE PERSON. Access granted
through a group never automaps, no matter how many times this is run. If they
get Full Access via a group, this tool cannot help and the answer is a direct
grant or a manually added mailbox in their profile.

WHAT IT DOES NOT FIX: an Outlook profile that has the mailbox added manually
already, a cached mode problem, or Send As. Only automapping.

## Calendar Permissions

<sub>`CalendarPermissions.ps1` &nbsp;|&nbsp; Tier 2 &nbsp;|&nbsp; works on: Mailbox</sub>

See and change who can view or edit someone's calendar.

Shows the current permission for each person who has one, and lets you add,
change or remove access at the usual levels -- from free/busy only through to
full editing.

The most common ticket this answers is "my assistant can't see my calendar"
or "someone can see more of my calendar than they should".

## Calendar Processing

<sub>`CalendarProcessing.ps1`</sub>

How a room decides what to do with a meeting request: accept it, decline it,
hold it for someone to approve, and what the reply says.

This is where "the room accepts everything", "the room declines recurring
meetings", and "nobody ever approves the bookings" are actually decided.

AutomateProcessing is the master switch and worth understanding before you
change anything else:
  AutoAccept    -- the room books itself by the rules below
  AutoUpdate    -- requests are tentatively marked, a delegate decides
  None          -- nothing is automatic; the mailbox behaves like a person
Most of the other settings only take effect under AutoAccept.

BookInPolicy / RequestInPolicy / RequestOutOfPolicy hold lists of people, and
they interact with the AllBookInPolicy / AllRequestInPolicy switches. Setting
a list while the matching All- switch is still true does nothing visible.

Editing writes with Set-CalendarProcessing immediately. There is no undo.

## Calendar Reset

<sub>`CalendarReset.ps1`</sub>

**Runs against:** reads the calendar's permissions. Apply REMOVES all of them and grants the two lists. Preview first.

"Clear the calendar and give Editor to these people and Reviewer to those."

This started as a one-off script and came up a fourth time. Paste names or
addresses, one per line, into the two boxes. Preview shows what will be
removed and what will be granted. Apply does it.

WHAT "CLEAR" MEANS HERE. Every explicit calendar permission is removed. Full
Access, Send As and the rest of the mailbox are NOT touched -- this is the
calendar folder only. For a full mailbox reset use Mailbox Permissions.

DEFAULT AND ANONYMOUS ARE SET, NOT REMOVED -- every folder has them and
Exchange refuses to delete them. The Default checkbox decides whether Default
is set to None (nobody outside the lists sees anything, not even busy blocks)
or left as it is (usually AvailabilityOnly -- free/busy for the company).
That is a decision about what everybody else can see, so it is a checkbox
and not a default.

NAMES ARE RESOLVED BEFORE ANYTHING IS REMOVED. A list with a typo in it is
found at Preview, not after the calendar has already been cleared.

Exchange Online only.

## Change Meeting Organizer

<sub>`ChangeMeetingOrganizer.ps1`</sub>

Moves a meeting or series from one organizer to another -- the usual case
being someone leaving who owns a recurring meeting nobody else can edit.

Look up the CURRENT organizer, type the subject, name the new organizer,
press Preview, then Transfer.

READ THIS BEFORE USING IT ON A TEAMS MEETING. Changing the organizer does NOT
change the organizer of the Teams online meeting attached to it. The new
organizer will not be able to manage or start that Teams meeting and must
replace the online meeting details manually afterwards.

WHO NOTICES:
  Attendees in this tenant  -- nothing. Silently updated, no re-RSVP.
  External / on-premises    -- a cancellation from the old organizer and a
                               new invitation from the new one. They must
                               re-RSVP, and any Reminder / Category / Show As
                               changes they made are lost.

ONE WAY, ONCE. After a transfer you cannot transfer the part of the series
left behind on the original calendar again.

Only user mailboxes, only the default calendar. Shared and room mailboxes are
not supported -- give the new person access to the mailbox instead.

## Convert Mailbox Type

<sub>`ConvertMailboxType.ps1`</sub>

**Runs against:** reads one mailbox's type. Convert changes it and asks first.

Disable-User converts a departing person's mailbox to shared as part of a
whole offboarding. This does ONLY the conversion, for the two asks that are
not an offboarding:

  "They've left, keep the mailbox as shared for the team, don't disable
   anything else."                                        -> To Shared

  "We hired them back, make it a normal mailbox again."   -> To User

THE LICENCE IS THE THING TO KNOW ABOUT.

  To Shared   A shared mailbox under 50 GB needs NO licence. The person's
              licence can be removed AFTER the conversion -- not before, or
              the mailbox is deleted with them. This tool does not remove the
              licence; it tells you when you can.

  To User     A user mailbox MUST be licensed. Without one it works for a
              30-day grace period and is then disabled. Assign the licence
              first, then convert. This tool checks nothing about licences
              because it cannot see them from Exchange alone -- it warns and
              trusts you.

Also handles Room and Equipment, because a shared mailbox that should have
been a room is a recurring one.

Exchange Online only. The conversion syncs to on-premises as an attribute
change; nothing here writes to Active Directory.

## Enable Archive

<sub>`EnableArchive.ps1`</sub>

**Runs against:** reads the on-premises remote-mailbox record. Enable changes it and asks first.

"Mailbox is full."  MBX-Stats says where the space went; this is the fix.

An online archive is a second mailbox in the cloud that the retention policy
moves old mail into. It is the answer to "full" that does not involve asking
somebody to delete things, and it needs a licence that most user plans
already include.

ENABLED ON-PREMISES, NOT IN THE CLOUD, AND THAT IS NOT OPTIONAL.

In a hybrid directory the on-premises object is the source of truth. Enabling
the archive in Exchange Online directly sets msExchArchiveGuid there; the next
directory sync writes the on-premises value -- which is empty -- back over it,
and the archive is disconnected. New User enables archives with
Enable-RemoteMailbox -Archive for exactly this reason, and this tool does the
same thing for a mailbox that already exists.

So: this runs on-premises, and the archive appears in the cloud after a
directory sync cycle. Mailbox Health shows both sides' ArchiveGuid; when they
match, it is done.

Cannot be undone from here. Disable-RemoteMailbox -Archive exists, but an
archive with mail in it is not something to switch off from a button.

## External Forwarding

<sub>`ExternalForwarding.ps1`</sub>

Finds mail leaving the organisation, from BOTH places it can be set up:

  * mailbox forwarding, configured by an admin or by the user
  * inbox rules, which users create themselves and which are the ones nobody
    thinks to check

The classic sign of a compromised mailbox is a quiet rule forwarding
everything to an outside address. This is the report that finds it.

Writes a CSV. Read-only.

## External Sharing

<sub>`ExternalSharing.ps1`</sub>

Reports how each SharePoint site is configured for external sharing, and which
guest accounts actually have access.

Both halves matter and neither is enough alone: a site permitting external
sharing with no guests on it is a setting, while a guest with access to a site
is a person who can read your files.

Writes a CSV. Read-only.

## Forwarding Editor

<sub>`ForwardingEditor.ps1`</sub>

**Runs against:** reads one mailbox's forwarding. Apply changes it and asks first.

"Forward Bob's mail to Alice while he's out."  "Stop forwarding it."

Mailbox Health SHOWS forwarding. Returning User CLEARS it. This SETS it.

THERE ARE TWO FORWARDING FIELDS AND THEY BEHAVE DIFFERENTLY:

  Internal (ForwardingAddress)      a recipient in OUR directory. Honours
                                    transport rules and is what you want for
                                    one colleague covering another.
  External (ForwardingSmtpAddress)  any address. This is the one that trips
                                    the outbound-spam policy: Exchange Online
                                    BLOCKS automatic forwarding to external
                                    addresses by default, and a forward that
                                    is set but blocked looks exactly like a
                                    forward that works until somebody asks
                                    where their mail went.

This tool picks the field for you: an address that resolves in the directory
goes in Internal, anything else goes in External and gets the warning.

KEEP A COPY decides whether mail also stays in the original mailbox. Off
means the mailbox stops receiving anything -- the usual mistake when the
person comes back and finds three weeks of nothing.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT TOUCH: inbox rules that forward. Those are per-user and
live in Inbox Rules. A mailbox can be forwarding through a rule while this
tool says it is not.

Exchange Online only.

## Grant External Access

<sub>`Grant-ExternalAccess.ps1`</sub>

**Runs against:** WRITES a Teams external access policy assignment. Changes configuration.

Assign a Teams external access policy to one user.

External access controls whether somebody can chat and meet with people
outside the organisation. This grants the policy that allows it.

THIS WRITES. It changes the user's Teams policy assignment, so it shows you
what they have now, asks, and then verifies the change actually took.

THE CURRENT POLICY IS SHOWN BEFORE YOU GRANT. That matters more than it
looks: a blank policy means the user is on the ORGANISATION-WIDE DEFAULT, and
granting an explicit policy takes them off it permanently. If the global
default is later changed, this user will not follow it.

ASSIGNMENT IS NOT INSTANT. Teams policy changes usually apply within minutes
but can take several hours to reach the client. A user reporting no change
ten minutes later is normal, and re-running this will not speed it up.

THE DOMAIN IS A FIELD, NOT A CONSTANT. It defaults to the tenant's primary domain. If
the user is on another accepted domain, change it rather than typing the
whole address -- the field is what gets appended.

It needs the MicrosoftTeams module and a connected Teams session.

## Hold Retention

<sub>`HoldRetention.ps1`</sub>

**Runs against:** reads one mailbox's hold and retention settings. Apply changes them and asks first.

Mailbox Health SHOWS holds. This one SETS them.

THREE SETTINGS, AND THEY DO DIFFERENT THINGS:

  Litigation hold    Nothing in the mailbox can be permanently deleted while
                     it is on -- not by the user, not by retention, not by
                     emptying anything. This is the legal-hold switch.
                     Duration is in days from when each item was received;
                     blank means indefinite.

  Retention policy   Which set of retention tags applies: how long things
                     stay before they are archived or deleted. The list comes
                     from the tenant.

  Retention hold     PAUSES the retention policy without removing it. For
                     someone on long leave whose mail should not be aged out
                     while they are away.

LITIGATION HOLD NEEDS A LICENCE. Exchange Online Plan 2, E3, E5, or the
Exchange Online Archiving add-on. On a mailbox without one, Set-Mailbox
refuses and this tool shows you the refusal rather than a green tick.

TAKING A HOLD OFF is the consequential direction: anything the hold was
keeping becomes deletable again, and retention catches up on the next pass.
The confirmation says so.

Exchange Online only.

## Hybrid Attribute Check

<sub>`HybridAttributeCheck.ps1` &nbsp;|&nbsp; works on: Mailbox</sub>

**Runs against:** reads Get-RemoteMailbox on-premises and Get-Mailbox / Get-EXOMailbox in the cloud for each identity you list. Changes nothing.

Side-by-side check of the attributes a hybrid mailbox needs to agree on.

In a hybrid the on-premises remote mailbox stub and the Exchange Online
mailbox are two objects describing one person. When they drift apart mail
usually keeps flowing, so nobody notices until a move fails, an archive
stops being reachable, or a reply to an old message bounces. This tool puts
the two objects next to each other and marks every line OK, MISMATCH or
MISSING.

Paste one or more identities (address or alias, one per line), or let the
console fill in the selected mailbox, and click Check. For each identity:

  * Exists              -- is there a stub on-premises, is there a mailbox
                           in the cloud
  * ExchangeGuid        -- must match, or the mailbox cannot be moved
  * ArchiveGuid         -- must match when there is an archive
  * RemoteRoutingAddress-- the stub's routing address must be one of the
                           cloud mailbox's addresses, or on-premises mail
                           for this person goes nowhere
  * PrimarySmtpAddress  -- the two primaries should be the same
  * EmailAddresses      -- smtp proxy addresses only on one side are listed
  * RecipientTypeDetails-- RemoteUserMailbox pairs with UserMailbox, and so
                           on for Shared, Room and Equipment

A read that fails for a reason other than "not found" is an ERROR row with
the message, so a dropped session never reads as a missing mailbox.

Read-only. Needs both Exchange Online and on-premises Exchange. Export
writes the grid to CSV.

## Mail Attributes (Rename)

<sub>`MailAttributes.ps1` &nbsp;|&nbsp; Tier 3 &nbsp;|&nbsp; works on: Mailbox</sub>

**Runs against:** reads on open. Every change asks first and says exactly what it will do.

View and edit the mail-related attributes on an account -- addresses, display
name, alias, and how the person appears in the address book.

THIS IS THE RENAME TOOL. Someone marries, changes name, or was created with a
typo: change the display name, the alias and the primary SMTP address here,
and keep the old address as a secondary so mail sent to it still arrives.

EVERYTHING HAPPENS ON-PREMISES and syncs to the cloud on the next cycle
(usually within 30 minutes). Nothing here touches Exchange Online, because on
a synced object the cloud copy is not the authoritative one -- an edit made
there is reverted on the next sync.

THE EMAIL ADDRESS POLICY IS THE THING THAT CATCHES PEOPLE OUT. If the account
is subject to an email address policy -- which is the default -- Exchange
generates its addresses from that policy and will not let you pin a different
primary. The tool reads that flag, shows it, and will not pretend to set a
primary address that the policy is going to regenerate. To change the primary
on such an account you have to detach it from the policy first, and the tool
asks you to confirm that explicitly, because from then on that account's
addresses are yours to maintain by hand.

ALIAS BEHAVES DIFFERENTLY DEPENDING ON THE OBJECT, and this is Microsoft's
documented behaviour rather than a quirk of the tool:
  - Remote mailbox (mailbox in the cloud, account on-premises): changing the
    Alias does NOT change the primary address.
  - On-premises mailbox subject to a policy: changing the Alias DOES
    regenerate the primary address.
The tool works out which kind of object it is looking at and says so.

WHAT IS DELIBERATELY READ-ONLY:
  UserPrincipalName        sign-in name; changing it affects far more than
                           mail and belongs in its own confirmation flow.
  RemoteRoutingAddress     the routing pointer to the cloud mailbox. Getting
                           it wrong is a mail-flow outage, not a typo.
  WindowsEmailAddress      Microsoft documents this as having NO effect while
                           the account is subject to an email address policy.
                           An edit that silently does nothing is worse than
                           no edit button.
  EmailAddresses           edit 'Primary SMTP' to change the primary, or use
                           'Add Secondary' to add one. Hand-editing the whole
                           collection is how the SMTP:/smtp: casing gets lost.

## Mail Contacts

<sub>`MailContacts.ps1`</sub>

**Runs against:** reads the contact. Apply creates, updates or removes it on-premises, and asks first.

A mail contact is an EXTERNAL address that shows up in the company address
book -- a vendor, an auditor, outside counsel, an external contact's personal
address. It has no mailbox and no login here; mail to it goes out to wherever
it really lives.

CREATED ON-PREMISES AND SYNCED UP, like every other object this toolkit
makes in a hybrid directory. Allow a sync cycle before it appears in the cloud
address book.

THE EXTERNAL ADDRESS MUST BE A FULL ADDRESS WITH ITS OWN DOMAIN. A bare name
would get the company domain appended, which is the opposite of what a
contact is for, so this tool refuses it rather than guessing.

  Add      creates it. Directory decides the OU, as in Mail Object.
  Update   changes the display name or the external address on one that exists.
  Remove   deletes it. Nothing is soft-deleted; a contact has no mailbox to
           keep. It is recreated in thirty seconds if that was a mistake.

Preview first. Apply does what Preview said.

## Mailbox / Onedrive Perms

<sub>`MailboxOneDriveAccess.ps1`</sub>

Grants or removes access to somebody's mailbox and their OneDrive, in one
place.

The usual case is someone leaving or being off unexpectedly, when their
manager needs both. Doing them separately is how one of the two gets
forgotten.

  * Mailbox -- Full Access and Send As
  * OneDrive -- site collection administrator on their personal site

OneDrive access is visible to the person if they return. It is appropriate for
a departure, less so for a temporary absence, and either way it should be
removed when it is no longer needed.

## Mailbox Perm Dupe

<sub>`MailboxPermDupe.ps1`</sub>

**Runs against:** reads the source mailbox, then GRANTS the same access on the target. Preview first; nothing is written until Apply.

"Give the new person the same access the old one had."

Reads five kinds of access off a SOURCE mailbox and grants them on a TARGET:

  Full Access        Get-/Add-MailboxPermission
  Send As            Get-/Add-RecipientPermission
  Send on Behalf     the GrantSendOnBehalfTo property on the mailbox
  Inbox              folder permissions on the Inbox
  Calendar           folder permissions on the Calendar

IT ADDS. IT NEVER REMOVES.

Access already on the target stays. If the target has a delegate the source
does not, that delegate is left alone. This is a copy, not a sync -- there is
no mode that makes the target match the source exactly, deliberately, because
"make these identical" on a live mailbox removes access somebody is using and
there is no undo button in this window.

WHAT IT WILL NOT COPY, AND WHY:

  NT AUTHORITY\SELF   every mailbox has it; it means "the owner". Copying it
                      would try to grant the SOURCE owner access to the
                      target, which is not what anybody means.
  Inherited entries   they come from the container, not from a decision made
                      about this mailbox. The target inherits its own.
  Deny entries        a deny copied out of context is a support ticket.
  The target itself   a mailbox does not need Full Access to itself.

FULL ACCESS IS GRANTED WITH AUTOMAPPING OFF. Exchange does not report the
source mailbox's AutoMapping setting through Get-MailboxPermission, so it
cannot be copied faithfully. Off is the choice that cannot surprise anyone --
with it on, a copy silently mounts the mailbox in the Outlook profile of every
delegate. Add it by hand afterwards if somebody needs it.

PREVIEW SHOWS EVERY GRANT BEFORE ANY OF THEM HAPPEN, and marks the ones that
are already present on the target so you can see what is actually new.

ONE FAILED GRANT DOES NOT STOP THE REST. Each is applied on its own and
reported on its own; the run finishes and tells you what did not work.

## Mailbox Permissions

<sub>`MailboxPermissions.ps1` &nbsp;|&nbsp; Tier 2 &nbsp;|&nbsp; works on: Mailbox</sub>

Grant, view or remove access to somebody else's mailbox.

Two different things, often confused, both handled here:

  * Full Access -- open and read the mailbox
  * Send As -- send mail that appears to come from the mailbox

They are granted separately. "I can see the shared mailbox but can't send from
it" is Full Access without Send As, and is the most common ticket in this area.

Changes are written to the audit log. Access granted here does not expire --
remove it when it is no longer needed.

## Migration Status

<sub>`MigrationStatus.ps1` &nbsp;|&nbsp; Tier 2 &nbsp;|&nbsp; works on: Mailbox</sub>

**Runs against:** the Exchange Online migration service. Reads batches and move requests; WRITES only when you press Complete, Start, Stop, Resume, Suspend, Remove or Set bad-item limit and answer Yes.

The state of hybrid mailbox moves, in two tabs.

  Batches       -- every migration batch with its counts. "Batch details"
                   shows the batch report. Start, Stop and Complete act on
                   the selected batch after a preview and a Yes.
  Move requests -- the move for one mailbox (or every move if the box is
                   blank). Statistics are fetched per SELECTED row, because
                   that call is slow and the question is nearly always about
                   one mailbox. "Details" shows the last 40 report entries.
                   Resume, Suspend and Set bad-item limit act on the
                   selected move. Exchange Online retired -BadItemLimit; on
                   a build without it the same button offers to approve the
                   skipped items instead, which is what unblocks a cloud move.

Refuses to remove a move request unless its Status is Completed.
Every write previews, asks, and is written to the audit log.
"Save CSV" writes the visible grid to the Reports folder.

## Missing Remote Mailbox

<sub>`MissingRemoteMailbox.ps1`</sub>

**Runs against:** reads every user mailbox in the cloud and every remote mailbox on-premises. Changes nothing.

Finds people whose mailbox exists in the cloud but who have NO on-premises
remote mailbox object.

It happens when a starter is licensed without anyone telling us. The licence
provisions a mailbox in Exchange Online and everything looks fine to the
user -- mail arrives, Outlook works -- while the on-premises stub that the
rest of our process depends on was never created.

WHAT BREAKS LATER, NOT NOW:

  * scan-to-email, which routes through on-premises Exchange
  * the disable process, which works from the on-premises object

Neither fails at the time. They fail on the day somebody scans a document or
the day that person leaves, which is the worst day to find out.

IT ALSO REPORTS A SECOND FAULT, because the same comparison finds it: a stub
that EXISTS but whose ExchangeGuid does not match the cloud mailbox. Mail
still flows, so nothing looks wrong, but the mailbox cannot be moved and a
migration will fail on it later. Those rows are marked GUID MISMATCH.

USER MAILBOXES ONLY. Shared, room, equipment, scheduling and Microsoft 365
group mailboxes are out of scope -- they are provisioned differently and a
missing stub does not mean the same thing for them.

Writes a CSV. Read-only -- it tells you who to fix, it does not create
anything. Needs both Exchange Online and on-premises Exchange.

## Mobile Devices

<sub>`MobileDevices.ps1`</sub>

**Runs against:** lists the devices on one mailbox. Remove and Wipe change things and each asks first.

Phones and tablets that sync with a mailbox through ActiveSync or Outlook
mobile, with model, OS, last sync time and status.

TWO DIFFERENT ACTIONS, AND THE DIFFERENCE MATTERS:

  Remove partnership   Exchange forgets the device. It stops syncing. The mail
                       already on the phone STAYS on the phone. Use this for
                       an old phone the user replaced, or a device that
                       should never have been there.

  Wipe (account only)  Exchange tells the device to delete THIS ACCOUNT's
                       mail, contacts and calendar the next time it checks in.
                       Personal photos and other apps are untouched. Use this
                       for a departing employee's personal phone.

A FULL device wipe -- factory reset of everything -- is deliberately NOT
offered here. It is the right answer for a lost company-owned phone and the
wrong answer for anything else, and this tool cannot tell which it is looking
at. If you need it, that is a one-off script and a conversation first.

A wipe is QUEUED, not immediate. It runs when the device next connects, which
for a phone that has been switched off is never. The grid shows the wipe
status so you can see whether it has actually happened.

Departing-employee note: Disable-User does not do this. Run this first.

Exchange Online only.

## Pim Activation

<sub>`PimActivation.ps1`</sub>

NOT IN USE. Kept because it works, and only consent is missing.

This tenant will not consent to the Graph permissions self-activation needs
(PrivilegedEligibilitySchedule.Read.AzureADGroup and
PrivilegedAssignmentSchedule.ReadWrite.AzureADGroup are admin-consent
delegated permissions on the Microsoft Graph PowerShell app). Without them
there is no supported programmatic route -- PIM for Groups is a Graph-only
API, and the retired AzureADPreview cmdlets covered directory roles, not
groups.

Use activate.ps1 instead, which opens the portal in the admin profile.

If consent is ever granted, this file should work as written -- it was
verified against the Graph v1.0 reference on 2026-08-06.

---------------------------------------------------------------------------

Activates your eligible PIM group assignments, without going to the portal.

Lists the groups you are eligible for, shows which are already active, and
lets you activate the ones you need with a duration and a justification.

  * Justification is required -- your PIM policy may reject a request
    without one, and it is recorded either way.
  * A ticket number can be attached if your policy asks for one.
  * Some assignments need approval. Those come back as PENDING APPROVAL, not
    activated, and this tool says so rather than pretending otherwise.

IMPORTANT: activating changes your group membership, but sessions you have
ALREADY connected -- Exchange Online, SharePoint -- are still using the token
they were issued at connect time. Reconnect them afterwards or the new access
will not appear.

Nothing here grants access you did not already have. It activates eligibility
that has already been assigned to you.

## Protocols

<sub>`Protocols.ps1`</sub>

Reports which client protocols are switched on for every mailbox -- POP, IMAP,
ActiveSync, Outlook on the web and the rest -- and writes a CSV.

Useful for security review: legacy protocols are the ones most often used in
password-spray attacks, and this shows where they are still enabled.

Read-only. It changes nothing.

## Recover Deleted Items

<sub>`RecoverDeletedItems.ps1`</sub>

**Runs against:** searches one mailbox's deleted items. Restore puts selected items back where they came from. Nothing is deleted.

"I deleted an email and now it's gone."

Searches three places, in order of how far gone the item is:

  Deleted Items       still in the folder -- the user could get it back themselves
  Recoverable Items   emptied from Deleted Items, or shift-deleted. Outlook's
                      "Recover Deleted Items" sees this too, but not everybody
                      knows it exists
  Purged Items        deleted from Recoverable Items as well. Only a hold or a
                      retention policy keeps anything here, and only an admin
                      can see it

Narrow by subject, by date, by item type. Then tick the ones to bring back and
press Restore. Each item goes BACK TO THE FOLDER IT WAS DELETED FROM -- Exchange
remembers, and that is what LastParentPath in the grid shows you.

RESTORE IS PER ITEM, NEVER PER FILTER. Restore-RecoverableItems will happily
restore everything that matches a subject, and "everything matching 'Invoice'"
on a finance mailbox is not a thing to do by accident. This tool only ever
restores the exact items you ticked, by their EntryID.

The date filter is on LAST MODIFIED, not on received. For a deleted item that
is usually the deletion time, which is what people actually remember.

Exchange Online only.

## Rename User

<sub>`RenameUser.ps1`</sub>

**Runs against:** WRITES to on-premises Active Directory. Reads Exchange Online only to check the new address is free.

Changes the email identity of a user who has been renamed -- marriage, legal
name change, a mistyped address at onboarding.

FOUR ATTRIBUTES MOVE TOGETHER, and that is the whole point of doing it here
rather than in ADUC:

  userPrincipalName   what they sign in with
  mail                what the directory says their address is
  mailNickname        the alias Exchange builds addresses from
  proxyAddresses      every address the mailbox actually receives on

Change three of the four and you get a mailbox that receives mail at an
address the person cannot sign in with, or a sign-in that no longer matches
the mailbox. They are one change.

THE OLD ADDRESS IS KEPT. It is demoted from primary to secondary, so mail sent
to it still arrives. A rename that stops the old address working breaks every
reply to every message they sent before today.

X500 ADDRESSES ARE CARRIED ACROSS UNTOUCHED. They are what lets Outlook
resolve replies to historical mail, and rebuilding a proxy list without them
breaks those replies weeks later, long after anybody connects it to a rename.

NAMES ARE NOT TOUCHED. displayName, givenName, sn and sAMAccountName stay as
they are -- this tool changes what the person is ADDRESSED as, not what they
are called or how they log on.

THE CLOUD LAGS. This writes to Active Directory. Exchange Online will not show
the change until the next AAD Connect sync cycle, and the tool says so rather
than letting you conclude the write failed.

The state before the change is written to the reports folder before anything
is modified.

## Resource Delegates

<sub>`Resource-Delegates.ps1`</sub>

**Runs against:** Reads and WRITES ResourceDelegates on a room or equipment mailbox. Changes are immediate on Save.

The people who approve booking requests for a room, and how to change them.

Type a resource in the box at the top. AN ADDRESS OR JUST THE FIRST PART
WORKS -- "conf-room-3" is retried as "conf-room-3@<the tenant's primary
domain>" before it gives up, and the same applies to the delegates you add.

SEVERAL DELEGATES AT ONCE. The add box takes a list: one per line, or
separated by semicolons or commas. Paste a column out of a spreadsheet or a
recipient line out of Outlook. Spaces are NOT separators, because a display
name is a valid thing to type. Every entry is looked up before it goes on the
list, and the result box says which were added, which were already there and
which did not resolve -- the ones that failed stay in the box so you can
correct them without re-typing the rest. Ctrl+Enter adds.

DELEGATES ONLY DO ANYTHING WHEN AutomateProcessing IS AutoUpdate, and that
switch is on this form. All three values it can take:

  AutoUpdate  -- every request is held TENTATIVE and the delegates below
                 approve or decline it. If the list is empty, NOTHING IS EVER
                 APPROVED and the room looks permanently busy to everyone.
  AutoAccept  -- the room books itself by its booking policy. Nobody vets
                 anything; the delegates are stored and are not asked.
  None        -- nothing is automatic. Requests sit in the resource mailbox
                 until a person opens it and answers by hand.

THE TWO ARE SAVED TOGETHER, in one write, because either alone is a trap: a
list with the wrong mode does nothing, and AutoUpdate with an empty list stops
the resource being bookable at all. That combination is confirmed separately
and in different words, whether you reach it by removing the last delegate or
by switching the mode.

Calendar Processing remains the tool for everything ELSE about how a room
decides -- the reply text, recurring meetings, conflict rules. This form
carries only the one switch the delegate list depends on.

THE WHOLE LIST IS REWRITTEN ON SAVE, because that is the only thing Exchange
offers. If somebody else changes the delegates while this window is open, Save
refuses and asks you to reload rather than quietly reverting their work.

A DELEGATE THAT NO LONGER RESOLVES is shown as UNRESOLVED with the raw value
the service returned. It is usually a deleted account, and it is left exactly
as it is unless you remove it -- rewriting a value nobody can identify is how
a list gets quietly corrupted.

For delegates on a PERSON's mailbox, this is the wrong tool: that is folder
permissions and Send On Behalf, and User Defined Delegates does it.

## ResourceDuplicator

<sub>`ResourceDuplicator.ps1`</sub>

Copies a room or equipment mailbox: reads every setting off an existing
resource, creates a new one, and applies the same settings.

For when a new meeting room should behave exactly like an existing one --
booking rules, delegates, capacity, auto-accept behaviour. Copying is more
reliable than setting a dozen options by hand and hoping you remembered them
all.

Check the source resource is actually configured the way you want before
copying it. Its mistakes get copied too.

## Restore Mailbox

<sub>`RestoreMailbox.ps1`</sub>

**Runs against:** lists soft-deleted mailboxes. Both restore actions change things and ask first.

A deleted mailbox is not gone. Exchange Online keeps it for 30 DAYS as
"soft-deleted", and this tool is the way back.

Load with the filter blank and EVERY soft-deleted mailbox is listed; type
part of a name or address to narrow it. Tick the rows you want. Restore in
place takes every tick at once; Copy wants exactly one.

TWO WAYS BACK, AND WHICH ONE DEPENDS ON WHETHER THE PERSON STILL EXISTS:

  Restore in place   The mailbox comes back as itself, attached to its user.
                     This needs the USER ACCOUNT to still exist -- or to be
                     restorable from the Entra recycle bin. In a hybrid
                     directory that means the on-premises AD account. If
                     Disable-User deleted the AD account and a sync has run,
                     the user is gone from Entra and this will fail. It says
                     so rather than pretending.

  Copy into another  The CONTENTS go into a mailbox you name -- a manager's,
                     a shared mailbox, a fresh account for the returning
                     person. The soft-deleted mailbox is left alone. This
                     works whether or not the original user exists, and it
                     is the answer to "we need what was in there, not the
                     account".

The copy is a RESTORE REQUEST: Exchange queues it and works through it in the
background. Big mailboxes take hours. The Requests panel shows progress; you
do not need to keep this window open.

THE 30-DAY CLOCK IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS. The grid shows days remaining. A
mailbox at 2 days is a today problem.

Exchange Online only.

## Room List

<sub>`RoomList.ps1`</sub>

Why a room does not appear in Outlook's Room Finder.

The Room Finder does not list rooms. It lists ROOM LISTS, and then the rooms
inside them. A room mailbox that belongs to no room list is invisible there no
matter how correct the mailbox and its place record are -- and the symptom
people report is "the room does not exist", which points nowhere near this.

A room list is an ordinary distribution group flagged as a room list. It
cannot be flagged after the fact through this tool: a normal group converted
to a room list keeps behaving oddly in the Room Finder, so New is the safe
route and that is all this offers.

Membership changes take effect immediately, but Outlook and Teams cache the
Room Finder aggressively -- allow up to 24 hours before concluding it did not
work. Verify here rather than in Outlook.

## Room Place

<sub>`RoomPlace.ps1`</sub>

The room metadata behind Outlook's room finder -- capacity, floor, building,
devices, accessibility, tags.

This is NOT the same as the mailbox. A room has a mailbox (name, address,
permissions) and a "place" record (what the room is like), and only the place
record drives room suggestions. A room that never appears in a search usually
has an empty place record rather than a broken mailbox.

Editing writes with Set-Place immediately. There is no staging and no undo.

IN A HYBRID ORGANISATION some fields cannot be set here at all. If the room
mailbox originated on-premises and syncs up, Microsoft blocks Set-Place from
changing City, CountryOrRegion, GeoCoordinates, Phone, PostalCode, State and
Street -- those come from the on-premises directory and must be changed there
with Set-User or Set-Mailbox. This tool marks those rows rather than letting
you discover it from a failure.

## Room Regional

<sub>`RoomRegional.ps1`</sub>

The timezone a room thinks it is in, and the hours it considers bookable.

A room created without a timezone inherits one, and that is how a room ends up
accepting a 9am booking that shows as 3am to the people in it. Nothing errors;
the meeting is simply at the wrong time.

TWO TIMEZONES LIVE HERE and they are not the same setting:
  Regional TimeZone          -- how the mailbox stores and displays times
  Working hours TimeZone     -- the zone the working hours below are stated in
They should almost always match. When they do not, "only during working hours"
means something nobody intended, and this tool says so.

ScheduleOnlyDuringWorkHours in Calendar Processing depends entirely on the
working hours set here. Turning that on without checking these is how a room
starts declining bookings for no visible reason.

## Set Booking Policy

<sub>`Set-BookingPolicy.ps1`</sub>

Controls WHO is allowed to book a room.

Pick a room, add or remove people, apply. Everyone not on the list has their
request declined automatically.

Type an address or alias in the box and press Enter. Bare aliases work -- if
'jsmith' does not resolve on its own the tenant's own domain is tried before
giving up. Select a row and press Delete, or use Remove, to take someone off.

THE LIST ALONE DOES NOTHING. A room also carries a master switch,
AllBookInPolicy, and while it is True the room accepts bookings from everyone
and the list is ignored entirely. Restricting a room means setting BOTH. This
tool does that together, and says so before it writes.

An EMPTY list with restriction on means nobody can book the room at all. That
is a valid thing to want and a terrible thing to do by accident, so it is
confirmed separately.

## Transport Rules

<sub>`TransportRules.ps1`</sub>

Every mail flow (transport) rule in the organisation, in one searchable list.

READ ONLY. Nothing here changes a rule, enables one, or reorders anything.

WHY NOT EDIT HERE. A transport rule applies to every message the organisation
sends or receives, and Set-TransportRule has well over a hundred conditions
and actions. A form covering all of them would be the admin centre rebuilt
worse; a form covering some of them can only edit the rules it understands,
and would quietly drop the parts it does not. The admin centre's condition
builder is the one thing it genuinely does well. Author there.

WHAT THIS DOES BETTER:

  Search       one box, matched against the WHOLE rule -- name, description,
               every condition and every action. "Which rule mentions this
               domain" is one keystroke here and a long afternoon in EAC.
  Priority     the running order in a single list. Which rule wins is decided
               by this, and it is the thing EAC shows least clearly.
  Detail       every property the rule actually SETS, with the couple of
               hundred empty ones left out.
  Snapshot     the whole collection to a dated XML file. Mail flow has no
               change history, so a snapshot before anyone edits is the only
               way to answer "what did this look like last week".

TAKE A SNAPSHOT BEFORE CHANGING RULES, not after. It is the only version of
yesterday you will ever have.

## User-Defined Delegates

<sub>`UserDefinedDelegates.ps1`</sub>

**Runs against:** READS and WRITES mailbox folder permissions and Send On Behalf in Exchange Online.

Who has access to somebody's Inbox, Calendar, Tasks, Contacts and Notes --
and Send On Behalf -- with the ability to change it.

Type an alias, the first part of an address, or a whole address. Press Load.

THIS WRITES. Add, Change and Remove act immediately on the mailbox. Every one
asks first and names what it is about to do.

DEFAULT AND ANONYMOUS ARE NOT PEOPLE AND CANNOT BE REMOVED. They are the
baseline for everybody who has no explicit entry, so Exchange refuses to
delete them. Set them to None instead -- the tool does that automatically if
you press Remove on one.

SEND ON BEHALF IS NOT SEND AS. On Behalf shows the recipient "Bob on behalf of
Alice"; Send As is indistinguishable from Alice sending it herself. They are
different permissions in different places, and this tool only does the first.
Send As lives in Mailbox Permissions.

FOLDER NAMES ARE LOOKED UP, NOT ASSUMED. A mailbox created in another language
has a Calendar folder called something else, and "\Calendar" simply fails on
it. The real name is read from the mailbox each time.

THE ACCESS LEVELS THAT MATTER MOST:
  Reviewer          can read. The right answer for most calendar requests.
  Editor            can read, create, change and delete. Full working access.
  AvailabilityOnly  free/busy only, no detail. Calendar only.
  Owner             everything including changing permissions. Rarely correct.

# Groups and DLs

## Bulk Add Members (CSV)

<sub>`Member_BulkADD_CSV.ps1`</sub>

**Runs against:** Reads a distribution list, ADDS or REMOVES members in bulk from a CSV, and ADDS or REMOVES Send-As / Send-To for named users. Writes CSV/TXT/HTML reports.

Add or remove a lot of people from one distribution list, from a list of
addresses in a CSV.

THE ORDER OF WORK:

  1. Type the list address and press Validate DL. Its current membership
     loads on the right.
  2. Pick ADD or REMOVE.
  3. Press Create & Open CSV to get a blank template, paste one address per
     line under the Email header, SAVE it, then press Load Emails. An
     existing CSV or a plain text list can be picked with Browse instead.
  4. Press Preview members (dry run). Nothing is changed and every address
     gets a row saying what WOULD happen.
  5. Press Apply members from CSV.

THE TWO HALVES HAVE THEIR OWN BUTTONS, and nothing in this window applies to
both at once:

  Step 1  Preview members (dry run) / Apply members from CSV
  Step 2  Preview permissions       / Apply permissions

The buttons along the bottom are exports and housekeeping -- they act on
whatever the last operation put in the grid, whichever operation that was.

NOTHING IS THROWN AT YOU. Every address ends up with a row and a status:
Added or Removed in green, Already Exists or Not a Member in yellow, and
Invalid Format, Recipient Not Found or Failed in red. One bad address in two
hundred does not stop the other hundred and ninety-nine.

AFTER AN UPDATE the membership is re-read from Exchange -- not assumed -- and
everything just added is highlighted and flagged NEW.

EXPORT FAILURES writes only the addresses that did not apply, with the reason
for each, and leads with an Email column so the file can be pointed straight
back at Load Emails to retry just those. You are asked whether to include the
rows that needed no change.

SEND-AS AND SEND-TO, for a handful of named users, are the second half of
this window -- folded in from dl_send_to-as.ps1, which did one person at a
time. Type them in the Users box, one per line or separated by commas, pick
one of the six options, and press Preview permissions before Apply.

THE USERS BOX IS NOT THE CSV. Members come from a file because there are
often hundreds; delegations are typed because there are usually two or three.
Sharing one input between them would mean granting Send-As to everybody in a
three-hundred-line membership import by accident.

SEND-AS means mail appears to come from the list. SEND-TO means being allowed
to mail the list at all, which only matters when the list is restricted.

THE ONE THING TO UNDERSTAND BEFORE USING "ADD SEND-TO":

A list with an EMPTY allowed-sender list accepts mail from everyone. Adding
the first people to that list does not grant them anything -- it locks
everybody else OUT. The window checks for this and asks again, in plain
words, because the intention ("let these three mail the list") and the effect
("only these three may mail the list") are opposites. Removing the last
entries does the reverse and is also confirmed.

AND: the allowed-sender list does nothing unless "Require sender
authentication" is on. The Now-set line says which. If it reads OFF, adding a
sender changes nothing anybody will notice.

A LIST SYNCED FROM ON-PREMISES cannot have its allowed-sender list changed
here -- it is mastered in Active Directory and the next sync would put it
back. That is refused. Send-As is a cloud ACL and is allowed. Membership is
warned about but allowed, because cloud-writable synced lists do exist.

IT DOES NOT CONNECT. If the ExO indicator on the console is red, press
Connect-ExchangeOnline there first; this window will refuse and say so rather
than raising a sign-in prompt it cannot service.

## Bulk DL Membership

<sub>`Bulk-DLMembership.ps1`</sub>

Adds or removes a set of people across a set of distribution lists in one
go. Built for the DL cloud migration, where membership moves in batches.

Paste distribution lists in one box and users in the other. The operation
is every user against every list: ten users across four lists is forty
changes, and the preview tells you that number before anything runs.

  * Check  -- resolves everything and shows exactly what will happen
  * Run    -- does it, after a confirmation

Anything that will not resolve is named individually and skipped, rather
than failing the whole batch. Results are written to the audit log, one
row per person.

There is no undo. A removal is recoverable only by adding people back, and
the audit log is what tells you who was in what.

WHICH ENVIRONMENT IT WRITES TO DEPENDS ON HOW IT WAS OPENED.
