Opened from DL Manager, it follows the group: a synced group is edited
on-premises in its own window, a cloud-managed one is edited in Exchange
Online in the console's session. The banner at the top of the window always
names the environment it is about to write to -- read it before pressing Run.

It refuses to run in a process where BOTH environments are loaded, because
the cmdlet names are shared and the wrong one would answer silently.

## DL Memberships

<sub>`DLMemberships.ps1` &nbsp;|&nbsp; Tier 2 &nbsp;|&nbsp; works on: Mailbox</sub>

**Runs against:** Reads group membership from Exchange Online. Changes nothing.

Shows every distribution list a person belongs to.

Answers "why is this person getting this mail" and "what will they stop
receiving when they leave" -- the second one is worth checking before a
termination rather than after.

Type an address and press Look Up. It is a single filtered query and should
come back in a second or two, however many groups the tenant has.

DIRECT MEMBERSHIPS ONLY. If Barney is in "All Staff" because "Accounts" is in
"All Staff", this lists Accounts and not All Staff. That is a real limitation
and the reason a person can still receive mail from a list that is not shown
here.

Microsoft 365 groups and dynamic distribution groups are not included --
dynamic groups have no stored membership to query, they are evaluated when
mail is sent.

Read-only. To change membership, use DL Manager or Bulk DL Membership.

## DL to Shared Mailbox

<sub>`DLtoSharedMB.ps1`</sub>

**Runs against:** step 1 reads. Steps 2, 3, 4 and 5 change things; 2, 3 and 5 ask first.

"Make legal@ a shared inbox instead of a distribution list."

The address has to move from a group to a mailbox, and the two cannot exist
at once. So: capture everything about the list, delete it, wait for a sync
so the cloud forgets the address, create the mailbox on-premises with the
same address, wait for a sync so the cloud has the mailbox, then grant the
old members access in the cloud.

  1  EXPORT (on-premises)   Every attribute of the list -- owners, members,
                            every proxy address, LegacyExchangeDN (the X500
                            that keeps replies to old mail working), sender
                            restrictions, custom attributes, Send As -- to a
                            CSV in the reports folder. Read only.
  2  DELETE (on-premises)   Distribution group: Remove-DistributionGroup.
                            Mail-enabled SECURITY group: Disable- only -- the
                            group may secure shares or apps, so it is kept and
                            just loses its address. Needs step 1 done in
                            this window. Then WAIT for a sync (30 min) and
                            press CHECK SYNC: one Get-Recipient in the cloud
                            on the list's address. "Still exists" -- wait;
                            "deleted" -- Create unlocks. After step 3 the same
                            button reports when the new mailbox has arrived.
  3  CREATE (on-premises)   Load the report (newest for this list is picked
                            for you), confirm the OU, account name and OWNER,
                            press Create. New-RemoteMailbox -Shared with the
                            list's address, then every proxy, the X500, the
                            hidden/restriction/custom attributes, and the
                            owner as the account's Manager -- all pinned to
                            a writable DC in the OBJECT'S OWN DOMAIN (from
                            its DN via Tenant.json), so a session parked on
                            another domain's DC can neither lose it nor get
                            a referral. WAIT for a sync.
  4  STAMP (on-premises)    The same stamp, on its own button, repeatable:
                            if step 3 reported a FAIL line, press this.
                            Adds only what is missing.
  5  PERMISSIONS (cloud)    Load the same report. Every former member and
                            owner gets Full Access and Send As; Send on Behalf
                            carries over; sent-items copy is turned on for
                            both Send As and Send on Behalf. Idempotent --
                            grants already present are reported, not
                            repeated.

OWNER IS REQUIRED. If the list had owners they are pre-filled; if not, you
must name one before Create is allowed. A shared mailbox with nobody
responsible for it is how a shared mailbox becomes nobody's.

The OU defaults to the directory's shared-mailbox OU from Tenant.json
(Tenant Manager, "Shared mbx OU"); it is editable here.

Steps can be run in different sessions: 3 and 4 start from the report file,
not from memory.

## Dynamic DL Preview

<sub>`DynamicDLPreview.ps1` &nbsp;|&nbsp; Tier 1 &nbsp;|&nbsp; works on: Mailbox, UnifiedGroup, OnpremGroup</sub>

**Runs against:** Exchange Online only. Reads dynamic distribution groups and recipients. Changes nothing.

Shows who a dynamic distribution group resolves to RIGHT NOW, and whether a
given person is in that list.

A dynamic group has no member list. Exchange evaluates its recipient filter
every time a message is sent, so "why did / didn't I get that email" cannot
be answered from the group object alone. This tool runs the same evaluation
Exchange does -- Get-Recipient with the group's RecipientFilter and
RecipientContainer -- and puts the result in a grid.

Load groups, pick one, Preview members. Type an address in the "Is this
person in it?" box and Check: the answer is YES or NO, matched on the
person's primary SMTP address against the preview.

Display is capped at 5000 rows; the CSV export and the person check use the
full result. Read-only. Never changes a group, a filter or a recipient.

## Group Editor

<sub>`GroupEditor.ps1` &nbsp;|&nbsp; Tier 3 &nbsp;|&nbsp; works on: UnifiedGroup, OnpremGroup</sub>

View and change who owns and who belongs to a group -- both Microsoft 365
groups and on-premises groups synced to the cloud.

Look the group up, then add or remove owners and members. Owners matter more
than they look: a group with no owner cannot be managed by anyone except an
admin, and nobody gets told when the last one leaves.

Changes take effect immediately and are written to the audit log.

## Group Manager

<sub>`Group-Manager.ps1`</sub>

**Runs against:** Reads one group from Exchange Online and opens another tool. Changes nothing.

Start here for any group -- distribution list, mail-enabled security group, or
Microsoft 365 Group.

Look the group up and this window tells you two things: WHAT it is, and WHERE
it lives. Then it opens the right editor for that combination, so you do not
have to know which of three tools to pick.

  Distribution list, synced     Group Manager Editor, against on-premises
  Distribution list, cloud      Group Manager Editor, against Exchange Online
  Microsoft 365 Group           Group Editor -- members and owners

A MICROSOFT 365 GROUP IS A DIFFERENT ANIMAL, and that is why it gets its own
destination. Access to one comes from MEMBERSHIP, not from mailbox permissions,
and it is managed with a completely separate family of cmdlets
(*-UnifiedGroup) that the distribution-list editor cannot speak.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN IT USED TO. During the migration, groups move from
on-premises to cloud a batch at a time. A group that needed the on-premises
editor last week may need the cloud one today. Nothing about the group's name
or address changes when that happens, so there is no way to tell by looking.

THE FAILURE THIS PREVENTS IS SILENT. Editing a converted group in the
on-premises tools does not produce an error. The change is written to Active
Directory, Active Directory is no longer the authority for that group, and
the change never reaches Exchange Online. It looks exactly like success.

The banner colour says whether the lookup WORKED, not where the group lives:
  GREEN  -- found. The line itself says cloud-managed or synced.
  RED    -- not found in Exchange Online, so there is nothing to route to.

Read-only. This window changes nothing itself; it only opens other tools.

## Group Manager Editor

<sub>`Group-Manager-Editor.ps1`</sub>

**Runs against:** One distribution group, in the environment named in the title bar.

One group, every setting, one window.

The title bar says [CLOUD] or [ON-PREMISES]. That is decided by DL Manager
from the group itself, not by you, and it is the difference between a change
that takes effect and one that is silently discarded.

FIVE SECTIONS, EACH APPLIED SEPARATELY. Nothing is written until you press the
Apply or Process button in that section, and each one confirms first.

  Owner            one person at a time. Owners matter more than they look:
                   a group with no owner can only be managed by an admin, and
                   nobody is told when the last one leaves.

  Membership       paste names into Add and Remove and process both at once.
                   Adds run before removals -- see below.

  Delivery         hidden from the address book, whether external senders are
                   accepted, and the allowed-senders list.

  Send-As          who may send mail that appears to come FROM the list.

THE ONE THING WORTH READING TWICE. An allowed-senders list does nothing on its
own. It is only enforced when 'Require sender authentication' is ON -- with it
off, the list is stored and ignored, and anyone can mail the group. This
window states which of the two situations you are actually in rather than
leaving you to work it out from two unrelated checkboxes.

There is no undo. Removals are recoverable only by adding people back, and
the audit log is what tells you who was there.

## New Cloud Group

<sub>`NewCloudGroup.ps1`</sub>

**Runs against:** Preview only reads. Create writes -- it asks first and shows exactly what it will do.

Creates a group in Exchange Online. Nothing on-premises is touched, and the
group does not sync down -- it exists only in the cloud.

TWO TYPES, AND THE DIFFERENCE MATTERS:

  Distribution group            Carries mail. Cannot be granted permissions
                                on anything. The right choice for a plain
                                "everyone in Accounts" list.
  Mail-enabled security group   Carries mail AND can be granted permissions
                                -- mailbox Full Access, Send As, SharePoint,
                                and so on. Choose this if the group will ever
                                be used to grant access to something.

YOU CANNOT CONVERT ONE INTO THE OTHER LATER. Exchange has no cmdlet for it;
the fix is to create the other kind and move the members. If you are unsure,
a mail-enabled security group does everything a distribution group does.

THE OWNER IS REQUIRED. A group with nobody responsible for it is a group
nobody prunes. By default the owner is also added as a member, which is what
the Exchange admin centre does and what people expect -- untick the box if
the owner should manage the group without receiving its mail.

EXTERNAL MAIL IS BLOCKED by default: only authenticated senders inside the
organisation can send to the group. Tick the box for a group that has to
receive mail from outside (info@, careers@, a supplier alias).

PRESS PREVIEW FIRST. It resolves the owner and every member, works out the
addresses, and checks that nothing already holds them -- all without
creating anything. Create is not enabled until Preview has passed.

## Unified Group Membership

<sub>`UnifiedGroupMembership.ps1`</sub>

**Runs against:** adds or removes members on Microsoft 365 groups. Changes membership.

Bulk membership for Microsoft 365 (Unified) groups -- many people, many
groups, in one go.

Paste addresses into the left box and group names or addresses into the
right. Add puts every person in every group; Remove takes every person out of
every group. Each pairing is applied on its own, so one bad address costs
that one pairing and not the batch.

THIS IS FOR MICROSOFT 365 GROUPS ONLY. Distribution lists and mail-enabled
security groups are a different object with a different cmdlet; for those
use Group-Bulk Management. A Microsoft 365 group shows as 'GroupMailbox' in
Unified Lookup -- a word containing 'Mailbox' and not 'Group', which is why
people end up in the wrong tool.

Exchange Online. Nothing touches Active Directory.

## UnifiedGroup Editor

<sub>`UnifiedGroup.ps1` &nbsp;|&nbsp; Tier 1 &nbsp;|&nbsp; works on: UnifiedGroup</sub>

View and edit the membership of a Microsoft 365 group.

Microsoft 365 groups are not distribution lists, even though they receive mail
like one. They also carry a Teams team, a SharePoint site and a shared mailbox,
so adding somebody here gives them more than an email feed.

Owners and members are separate lists and both matter -- see Group Editor if
you need to change ownership.

## dl send to as

<sub>`dl_send_to-as.ps1`</sub>

**Runs against:** Reads and WRITES Send-As and delivery restrictions on a distribution list in Exchange Online.

Give one person, or take away from them, the right to send AS a distribution
list or to send TO one.

TYPE THE LIST, TYPE THE PERSON, PICK ONE ACTION, PRESS APPLY. Either address
box accepts a full address or just the first part -- the tenant domain is
added for you.

SEND-AS means mail appears to come from the list. SEND-TO means being allowed
to mail the list at all, which only matters when the list is restricted.

THE ONE THING TO UNDERSTAND BEFORE USING "ADD SEND-TO":

A list with an EMPTY allowed-senders list accepts mail from everyone. Adding
the first person to that list does not grant them anything -- it locks
everybody else OUT. The window checks for this and asks again, in plain
words, because the operator's intention ("let Bob mail this list") and the
effect ("only Bob may mail this list") are opposites.

Removing the last entry does the reverse: the list goes back to accepting
mail from anyone. That is also confirmed.

AND THE OTHER THING: the allowed-senders list does nothing at all unless
"Require sender authentication" is on. The window shows that flag beside the
list. If it says OFF, adding a sender changes nothing anybody will notice.

A LIST SYNCED FROM ON-PREMISES cannot have its delivery restriction changed
here -- it is mastered in Active Directory and the next sync would put it
back. The window refuses and says so. Send-As is a cloud ACL and is allowed.

# Reporting

## Audit SMB

<sub>`AuditSMB.ps1` &nbsp;|&nbsp; Tier 2 &nbsp;|&nbsp; works on: Mailbox</sub>

**Runs against:** searches the Microsoft 365 audit log. Changes nothing.

The same audit-log search as Audit UserMB, for a shared mailbox -- plus the
thing that makes a shared mailbox a different question: WHO HAS ACCESS.

THIS IS NOT A SETTINGS REPORT. It returns what was actually done to the
mailbox, not what the mailbox is configured to record.

Before searching it lists everyone holding Full Access, so those names are on
screen while you read the events. On a shared mailbox the question is almost
never "what did the owner do" -- it is "which of the six people with access
did this", and that is unanswerable without the list beside it.

THREE THINGS THAT MAKE IT LOOK BROKEN WHEN IT IS NOT:

  * Entries can take 30+ MINUTES to appear. An action performed a moment ago
    legitimately will not be there yet, which is exactly when somebody tests
    it and concludes the tool does not work.
  * Default retention is 180 days, unless Audit (Premium) or a custom
    retention policy extends it. Older than that is gone, not hidden.
  * It needs the 'View-Only Audit Logs' or 'Audit Logs' role in Microsoft
    Purview, on top of an Exchange Online connection.

A wide date range on a busy mailbox takes minutes. It pages through the
result set and can be stopped part way -- you keep whatever came back, and
the window says so rather than pretending that was all of it.

Each row keeps its raw JSON alongside the parsed columns. The columns answer
most questions; the JSON answers the one they do not.

Read-only.

## Audit User Mailbox

<sub>`AuditUser.ps1` &nbsp;|&nbsp; Tier 2 &nbsp;|&nbsp; works on: Mailbox</sub>

**Runs against:** searches the Microsoft 365 audit log. Changes nothing.

Searches the audit log for what actually HAPPENED to a mailbox -- who opened
it, what they did, from where, and when.

THIS IS NOT A SETTINGS REPORT. It does not tell you what is being recorded;
it tells you what was recorded. "Who read that message", "did anyone else
send as this account", "what did the delegate do on Tuesday".

Pick a date range, optionally narrow to particular operations, and search.

THREE THINGS THAT MAKE IT LOOK BROKEN WHEN IT IS NOT:

  * Entries can take 30+ MINUTES to appear. An action performed a moment ago
    legitimately will not be there yet, which is exactly when somebody tests
    it and concludes the tool does not work.
  * Default retention is 180 days, unless Audit (Premium) or a custom
    retention policy extends it. Older than that is gone, not hidden.
  * It needs the 'View-Only Audit Logs' or 'Audit Logs' role in Microsoft
    Purview, on top of an Exchange Online connection.

A wide date range on a busy mailbox takes minutes. It pages through the
result set and can be stopped part way -- you keep whatever came back, and
the window says so rather than pretending that was all of it.

Each row keeps its raw JSON alongside the parsed columns. The columns answer
most questions; the JSON answers the one they do not.

Read-only. For a shared mailbox use Audit SMB, which does the same search and
also lists who holds Full Access.

## Bug Fix

<sub>`BugFix.ps1`</sub>

**Runs against:** Sends an email. Makes no changes to any mailbox, account, or group.

Report something that is broken.

A copy is sent to you, so you have a record of exactly what you reported.

THE FIELD THAT MATTERS MOST IS 'Steps to reproduce'. A bug that can be
reproduced is usually fixed the same day; one that cannot may never be. If you
only fill in one optional box, make it that one -- even "it happens on shared
mailboxes but not user ones" is enough to halve the search.

WHAT MAKES A REPORT EASY TO ACT ON:
  - The exact error text, pasted rather than described. "It said something
    about a domain controller" and the actual 0x52 message are different
    amounts of information.
  - What you EXPECTED. Half of all bug reports turn out to be the tool doing
    what it was built to do, and knowing what you expected instead is what
    turns that into a real answer rather than "working as designed".
  - Whether it happens every time. An intermittent fault and a constant one
    are chased completely differently.

IF IT IS BLOCKING YOU RIGHT NOW, tick the box. That is what gets looked at
first, and it is the only thing on this form that jumps the queue.

You do not need to know what caused it. Report it anyway.

## Cert Check

<sub>`CertificateExpiry.ps1`</sub>

Reports the certificates on every on-premises Exchange server and how long
each has left.

Worth running monthly. An expired certificate breaks hybrid quietly -- the
first symptom is usually somebody complaining that free/busy has stopped
working between on-premises and the cloud, which does not look like a
certificate problem.

Certificates in use are separated from ones that are just sitting there, since
only the first kind will break something.

Read-only. On-premises Exchange only.

## Clear IIS Logs

<sub>`Clear-IISLogs.ps1`</sub>

**Runs against:** DELETES IIS log files on on-premises servers over an admin share. Destructive.

Delete IIS log files older than a set age from the hub servers.

THIS TOOL DELETES FILES. It is the only one here that does. Read the rest of
this before running it.

HOW IT WORKS. Press Scan first. Nothing is deleted by scanning -- it lists
every file that WOULD go, with a total size, and only then does the Delete
button become available. Delete acts on exactly that list and nothing else,
so what you reviewed is what goes.

WHAT IT WILL TOUCH, AND NOTHING ELSE:
  *.log files only, in these two folders on each server:
      C:\inetpub\logs\LogFiles\w3svc1
      C:\inetpub\logs\LogFiles\w3svc2
  Not subfolders. Not other extensions. Not any other path.

WHY IT IS FUSSY ABOUT THE PATH. A typo in a log path that then gets deleted
recursively is unrecoverable, so the folder is checked to be one of the two
above before a single file is listed, and anything that is a junction or
symlink is skipped rather than followed -- a reparse point in a log folder
would take a delete somewhere nobody intended.

THIRTY DAYS IS A DEFAULT, NOT A RULE. Check what your retention policy
actually requires before lowering it. IIS logs are the evidence for "who
connected and when", and once they are gone that question cannot be answered.
If there is an incident open, do not run this.

AGE IS BY LastWriteTime, not by the date in the filename. A log still being
written to today keeps today's timestamp regardless of what it is called.

It needs admin share access (\\server\C$) to each server.

## Config Backup

<sub>`ConfigBackup.ps1`</sub>

Copies Config\*.json somewhere safe, and puts them back.

These are the files that are YOURS rather than the toolkit's: Tools.json,
Settings.json, Sections.json, QuickLaunch.json, Themes.json, Tenant.json.
Copying a new console folder over an old one replaces every one of them, and
nothing warns you -- the loss shows up later as blank paths and missing
buttons.

RUN A BACKUP BEFORE COPYING A NEW CONSOLE OVER THIS ONE. That is the whole
reason this exists.

Backups are written OUTSIDE the console folder, beside it, so that replacing
or renaming the console cannot take the backup with it. Each backup is a
timestamped folder holding the files exactly as they were.

Restore copies a backup back over Config\ -- and takes a fresh backup of what
is there first, so restoring the wrong snapshot is not final either.

## DL Inventory

<sub>`DLInventory.ps1`</sub>

Inventories the mail-enabled groups in on-premises Active Directory, for
migration planning. Writes a CSV.

Built for the distribution list move to the cloud: what exists, how big it is,
and who manages it, in one file you can sort and plan against.

Read-only.

## Diagnose AD Gate

<sub>`Diagnose-AdGate.ps1`</sub>

**Runs against:** Active Directory

Reports why the AD capability gate is open or closed on this machine: module present, domain reachable, rights held.
Read-only.

## Diagnose ExO Resolve

<sub>`Diagnose-ExoResolve.ps1`</sub>

**Runs against:** Exchange Online and on-premises Exchange

Shows how a recipient resolves in each place, for when a tool finds an object the operator cannot.
Read-only.

## Disabled/Licensed

<sub>`DisabledLicensed.ps1`</sub>

Finds accounts that are disabled in Active Directory but still sitting in a
licence group -- so they are still costing money.

Straightforward cleanup list, and usually a longer one than expected. Writes a
CSV.

Read-only. Removing the licence is a separate, deliberate step.

## Domain Mail Auth Check

<sub>`DomainMailAuthCheck.ps1`</sub>

**Runs against:** reads accepted domains and DKIM signing configs from Exchange Online, then queries public DNS for each domain. Changes nothing.

One grid answering "is mail authentication set up for this domain" for
every accepted domain in the tenant, or for one you pick.

Load domains reads Get-AcceptedDomain and Get-DkimSigningConfig. Run
checks then asks DNS, per domain:

  * MX      -- the records that exist. FAIL when there are none.
  * SPF     -- the TXT record starting v=spf1. FAIL when missing or when
               there is more than one (RFC 7208 allows exactly one), FAIL
               on +all, WARN on ?all or no all mechanism at all.
  * DKIM config      -- Enabled and Status from Get-DkimSigningConfig.
  * DKIM selector1/2 -- the selector1._domainkey and selector2._domainkey
               CNAMEs must resolve to the Selector1CNAME / Selector2CNAME
               values Exchange Online reports. Anything else is FAIL.
  * DMARC   -- the _dmarc TXT record. FAIL when missing, WARN on p=none,
               PASS on p=quarantine or p=reject.

Detail is the record actually found, so a FAIL can be read without
opening a DNS tool. Select a row to see the whole record in the box under
the grid.

DNS is asked through Resolve-DnsName (the DnsClient module, Windows 8 /
Server 2012 and later). System DNS is used unless you choose a public
resolver -- useful when the internal resolver answers for a domain it
hosts a split view of. Without the module the DNS rows say so and the
DKIM config rows still run.

Read-only. Export writes the grid to CSV.

## Exchange Health Check

<sub>`Exchange-HealthCheck.ps1`</sub>

**Runs against:** Reads services, queues, database copies and disks from on-premises servers. Read-only.

The health of the four hub servers, on five tabs. Press Run.

WHAT EACH TAB IS FOR:

  Summary & Server Overview   Start here. Every problem found across all the
                              other tabs, listed once, plus uptime and who
                              last rebooted each server.
  Services / IIS / Logging    Exchange services that are not running when they
                              should be, IIS state, and whether IIS logging is
                              actually writing.
  Database Copy Status        Mounted, healthy, and how far behind each copy
                              is. Copy and replay queues matter more than the
                              status word.
  Transport Queues            Queue lengths and anything retrying.
  Drive Space                 Free space per drive, worst first.

AUTOMOUNT AND CONTENTINDEXSTATE ARE NOT NOISE. A copy that is Healthy with a
failed content index cannot serve search, and a database that is mounted but
whose copies are all behind is a failover that will lose mail.

A SERVER THAT DID NOT ANSWER IS NAMED, not skipped. An empty row for a server
that is down looks exactly like a server with nothing wrong.

It needs WinRM to each server. Queue and database data additionally need the
Exchange management tools.

Read-only. It reports and changes nothing.

## Feature Request

<sub>`FeatureRequest.ps1`</sub>

**Runs against:** Sends an email. Makes no changes to any mailbox, account, or group.

Ask for something the console does not do yet.

Fill in the three boxes and press Send. The request is mailed off and a copy
lands in your own inbox, so you have a record of exactly what you asked for.

ANSWER THE FREQUENCY QUESTION HONESTLY. It is the field that decides what gets
built first. "Twice a day" and "once a quarter" are both fine answers -- a
small annoyance that happens constantly is usually worth more than a large one
that almost never does, and there is no way to know which yours is unless you
say. Guessing high does not help you; it just moves the queue around.

WHAT MAKES A REQUEST EASY TO ACT ON:
  - Describe the PROBLEM, not the solution you have in mind. "I have to open
    three tools to answer one ticket" leads somewhere better than "add a
    button here", because the button might not be the best fix.
  - Name the tool and the exact step, if it is about one tool.
  - Say what you do today instead. The workaround is often most of the design.

You do not need to know whether it is possible. Ask anyway.

## Free/Busy Viewer

<sub>`FreeBusyViewer.ps1`</sub>

**Runs against:** reads organization relationships, intra-organization connectors and configuration, and sharing policies from Exchange Online. "Test" runs Test-OrganizationRelationship for one user. Changes nothing.

"Why can't they see my calendar" lives in four places, and this window
shows all four:

  * Organization relationships -- federation with another Exchange
    organisation, and the hybrid relationship with on-premises. Domains,
    whether free/busy is on, at what level, and the endpoints it targets.
  * Intra-organization connectors -- the hybrid OAuth path, which takes
    over from the organization relationship for the on-premises side when
    it is present and enabled.
  * Intra-organization configuration -- what Exchange Online believes the
    on-premises target addresses and endpoints are.
  * Sharing policies -- per-user calendar sharing to outside domains,
    which is a different mechanism from the three above and is the one
    that governs "share my calendar with a partner".

Load reads all four. Select a row to see every property of it in the box
under the grids. Export writes the visible tab to CSV.

The Test tab runs Test-OrganizationRelationship for one relationship and
one user mailbox and shows every line the cmdlet produces, verbose and
warning output included -- that is where the useful part of the answer
is. It reads and verifies; it changes nothing.

Read-only throughout.

## Log Viewer

<sub>`LogViewer.ps1` &nbsp;|&nbsp; Tier 3</sub>

A read-only view of the audit log -- every change the toolkit's tools have
made, who made it, when, and to whom.

This is the answer to "when did that happen and who did it". Search and filter
across everything, including logs in the older format.

Nothing here changes anything. The log is the record; this reads it.

## M365 Reports

<sub>`M365Reports.ps1`</sub>

Buttons that open the Microsoft 365 admin portal reports -- usage, activity,
licensing, security -- in the browser.

These are reports Microsoft already computes, from data a script cannot get at
directly. Rather than reproduce them badly, this puts them one click away.

It opens each in the elevated Edge profile, so you are signed in as the right
account when you land.

Nothing is read or changed by this tool. It opens links.

## MB w No activity

<sub>`StaleAccounts.ps1`</sub>

Finds accounts that are enabled and licensed but have not signed in for a
while.

Two reasons to care: a licence being paid for and not used, and an account
nobody is watching that still works. Writes a CSV.

Not every result is dead -- shared and service accounts show up here
legitimately. Treat it as a list to review, not a list to disable.

Read-only.

## MBX Stats

<sub>`MBX-Stats.ps1`</sub>

**Runs against:** reads one mailbox's statistics. Changes nothing.

Where the space went. Total size against the quota, then the folders that
account for it.

The ticket this answers is "my mailbox is full" or "why can I not send", and
the useful answer is almost never the total -- it is which folder holds it.
Usually Deleted Items nobody ever emptied, or a Sent Items going back nine
years, or Recoverable Items quietly holding everything a retention policy
was asked to keep.

WHAT IT SHOWS:
  * total size, item count, and percentage of the send quota used
  * Inbox, Sent, Calendar and Deleted Items, called out first
  * every other well-known folder
  * the ten biggest folders anywhere in the mailbox
  * the archive, if there is one, on the same basis

RECOVERABLE ITEMS IS NOT A FOLDER THE USER CAN SEE, and it is the usual
reason a mailbox is far bigger than the sum of everything visible. It holds
deleted mail a hold or a retention policy is keeping. Emptying Deleted Items
does not shrink it. If that is where the space is, the answer is a retention
or hold question rather than a housekeeping one -- Mailbox Health shows which
holds are applied.

Read-only. Exchange Online.

## Mail Flow Connectors

<sub>`MailFlowConnectors.ps1` &nbsp;|&nbsp; Tier 2</sub>

**Runs against:** reads every inbound and outbound connector in Exchange Online. "Test outbound" sends ONE test message through the selected outbound connector, after asking.

Lists every Exchange Online inbound and outbound connector in one grid, with
the settings hybrid mail flow depends on: type, enabled state, sender or
recipient domains, smart hosts, TLS and certificate requirements.

Connectors are the part of hybrid mail flow nobody looks at until mail
stops. The Warnings box flags the handful of states that are unambiguously
worth a look -- a disabled connector, an on-premises connector routing by
MX record, an on-premises connector with no TLS or no certificate domain --
and says why in one line each.

Details shows every property of the selected connector. Export writes the
grid to CSV. Read-only, with one exception: "Test outbound" runs
Validate-OutboundConnector against the selected OUTBOUND connector, which
sends a real test message to an address you type. It asks first and logs
separately. Nothing is ever changed on a connector.

## Orphaned OneDrive

<sub>`OrphanedOneDrive.ps1`</sub>

Finds OneDrive sites whose owner is disabled or no longer in Active Directory.

When someone leaves, their OneDrive does not leave with them. It sits there
holding whatever they had, still consuming storage, with nobody responsible
for it.

Writes a CSV. Read-only -- deciding what to do with the content is a
conversation, not a script.

## Ownerless Groups

<sub>`OwnerlessGroups.ps1`</sub>

Finds Microsoft 365 groups with no effective owner.

An ownerless group cannot be managed by anyone but an admin -- nobody can add
members, change settings or delete it -- and it happens quietly whenever the
last owner leaves. Nobody is notified.

Writes a CSV. Read-only.

## Permissions Audit

<sub>`PermissionsAudit.ps1`</sub>

Reports every mailbox delegation across the organisation -- Full Access, Send
As and Send on Behalf. Writes a CSV.

Answers "who can get into what", which is a question that only ever gets asked
under time pressure. Access granted for a good reason years ago is still
access.

Read-only. It reports; it does not remove anything.

## Protocol Usage

<sub>`ProtocolUsage.ps1`</sub>

**Runs against:** reads every mailbox's protocol settings and a usage export you provide. Changes nothing.

Protocols.ps1 says what is ENABLED. This says what is USED.

Built to get a change request approved. "These are enabled on 4,000
mailboxes" is a configuration statement and invites the question that stops
the change: how do you know nobody needs them.

HOW TO USE IT
  1. Press "Open sign-in logs" and export the sign-in report from Entra,
     filtered to the legacy client apps. Or export the Email App Usage
     report from the M365 admin centre.
  2. Point this at the CSV.
  3. It reads the enabled state live, joins the two, and writes both a
     per-mailbox CSV and a summary paragraph you can paste into the ticket.

HOW FAR BACK YOU CAN ACTUALLY PROVE -- READ THIS BEFORE PROMISING A YEAR

  Entra sign-in logs      30 days. Not negotiable without a Log Analytics
                          workspace that was ALREADY collecting them.
  Email App Usage report  180 days maximum.

  Neither gives you a year. A year of evidence exists only if somebody set
  up log shipping before you needed it.

THE ARGUMENT THAT DOES NOT NEED A YEAR

  Microsoft REMOVED Basic authentication for POP, IMAP, ActiveSync, EWS and
  the rest in late 2022. Nobody has signed in to those with a password since.
  What the enabled flag still permits is POP/IMAP over OAuth, which is rare
  and which a 30-day sign-in export will show.

  So the case is: the dangerous half has been dead for three years, the
  surviving half has zero users in the window you can evidence, and the
  setting is on for N mailboxes with no consumer.

Read-only. Writes a CSV and nothing else.

## Report Browser

<sub>`ReportBrowser.ps1`</sub>

Opens any CSV the reporting tools have written, without going and finding it
in Explorer.

Every report writes a timestamped file to the reports folder. This lists them
all, newest first, across every report type, so you can re-read last month's
without re-running it.

Read-only.

## SMB Inventory

<sub>`SMB_Inventory.ps1`</sub>

**Runs against:** READS every shared mailbox in Exchange Online. Writes nothing.

Lists every shared mailbox in Exchange Online with the things that decide
whether it is safe to source-anchor to Microsoft 365.

For each mailbox:

  Anchored     CLOUD if it was created in Exchange Online, SYNCED if it comes
               from on-premises Active Directory. A synced mailbox is managed
               on-premises -- that is the one that needs the anchor moved.
  FullAccess   how many real people can open it. NT AUTHORITY\SELF and the
               other built-in entries are not counted -- they are noise and
               counting them makes every mailbox look busy.
  SendAs       how many real people can send as it.
  Restricted   whether anyone has set delivery restrictions -- an explicit
               accept-only or reject list.

PILOT COLUMN. "Easy" means synced, one or two Full Access delegates, and no
delivery restrictions. Those are the mailboxes with the fewest people to
notice if something goes wrong. Sort on that column and start at the top.

TWO THINGS THE PILOT COLUMN DELIBERATELY DOES NOT DO:

It does not count "blocks external senders" as a restriction. That setting is
on by default for most shared mailboxes, so treating it as a complication
would flag nearly everything and make the column useless. It is reported in
its own column instead.

It does not look at how BUSY a mailbox is. A mailbox with one delegate that
receives four hundred messages a day is not an easy pilot, and this report
cannot tell you that. Check the top candidates against message volume before
committing to them.

## Tool Status

<sub>`ToolStatus.ps1`</sub>

Lists every .ps1 beside the console and says what loads it.

  AdminConsole   -- a button in the console points at it.
  Dashboard      -- the dashboard can launch it.
  Not loaded     -- nothing opens it. Safe to park.
  Parked         -- already moved to DisabledTools.

Green means something loads it. Yellow means nothing does. Grey means it is
already parked.

Click the ? column, or double-click a row, to read that tool's own help --
the same text its own ? button shows. Yellow does not mean useless: a script
may be deliberately shelved, or called by another script rather than opened
by a button. Read it before parking it.

Last run comes from the audit log, so it is when the tool last did something
worth recording -- not when it was last opened.

Common.ps1, AdminConsole.ps1, Publish-Toolkit.ps1 and this tool are not
listed. They are infrastructure and must never be parked.

Parking MOVES a file to DisabledTools. It deletes nothing, and Restore puts
it back. This deployment keeps only what it uses; the master copy keeps
everything.

AFTER MOVING ANYTHING, RE-RUN Publish-Toolkit. The version manifest lists
files by name, so a parked script reads as missing until the toolkit is
re-stamped.

## Transport Queues

<sub>`Get-Queues.ps1`</sub>

**Runs against:** Reads transport queues from four on-premises Exchange servers. Read-only.

Every transport queue on the four hub servers, on one screen.

WHY THIS EXISTS. Get-Queue has no organisation-wide view -- it is one call per
server, and checking a mail-flow complaint means four logons or four windows.
By the time the fourth is open the first is out of date, so a queue that is
draining looks identical to one that is stuck.

WHAT MATTERS, IN ORDER:
  Status Retry      the queue cannot reach the next hop. This is the one.
  Status Suspended  somebody stopped it by hand and may have forgotten.
  A large MessageCount that is NOT falling between refreshes.

A BIG QUEUE IS NOT AUTOMATICALLY A PROBLEM. A queue of several hundred that is
shrinking is a queue doing its job. The number on its own tells you nothing --
press Refresh again and compare. That is why the count from the previous run
is shown beside the current one.

THE SUBMISSION AND SHADOW QUEUES ARE NORMAL. Shadow queues hold copies for
redundancy and sit at a steady non-zero count on a healthy server. Do not
chase them.

A SERVER THAT DID NOT ANSWER IS REPORTED, NOT SKIPPED. A silent omission here
would read as "that server has no queues", which is the opposite of the truth
when it is the one that is down.

Read-only. It reports and changes nothing -- it cannot retry, suspend or
delete a queue.

## onprem mailtest

<sub>`onprem-mailtest.ps1`</sub>

**Runs against:** SENDS real email through each on-premises hub server. Delivers mail.

Send a test message through each hub server, one at a time, and report which
ones accepted it.

THIS SENDS REAL EMAIL. It is not a simulation. Anything you put in the
recipient boxes will receive a message from you.

WHY TWO RECIPIENT BOXES. Internal and external delivery are different tests
and they fail independently:

  Internal   proves the server accepts mail and delivers inside the org.
  External   proves outbound relay, the send connector, and whatever sits in
             front of it. This is the one that breaks after a firewall or
             connector change, and an internal-only test will not notice.

Either box on its own is enough. Fill in both and each server sends two
separate messages, so a server that delivers internally but cannot relay out
shows as one pass and one fail rather than a single ambiguous failure.

EACH SERVER IS TESTED SEPARATELY and the server name goes in the subject, so
the messages that arrive tell you which route worked without reading this
grid. Doing them one at a time is the point -- if three deliver and one does
not, that names the broken server.

ACCEPTED IS NOT DELIVERED. A green row means the server took the message, not
that it arrived. Check the mailbox as well; a message can be accepted and then
dropped by a rule, a filter, or the receiving side.

ATTACHMENTS. 'Add files...' picks one or several; go again to add more from a
different folder. Double-click a row, or select rows and press Remove, to drop
them. Every test message carries the same files.

WATCH THE SIZE LINE, because the number that gets a message rejected is not
the number on disk. Attachments travel base64-encoded, which is about 1.37x
bigger, and that encoded size is what a connector limit is measured against --
a 20MB file will not pass a 25MB limit. The panel shows both, and the total
across every message queued, because one 10MB file to two recipients on four
servers is 80MB of real traffic.

IF A SEND FAILS ON SIZE the summary says so rather than leaving it looking
like a routing fault, and tells you to retry with nothing attached to prove
the route itself is fine. That distinction is the whole reason this box is
here: "mail is broken" and "mail is broken for a 30MB file" are different
problems with different owners.

# Projects

## AvePoint Dashboard

<sub>`AvePoint-Dashboard.ps1`</sub>

**Runs against:** AvePoint

Executive and compliance view built from the AvePoint API.
Read-only: it reports what AvePoint knows and changes nothing.

## Hybrid Message Trace

<sub>`HybridMessageTrace.ps1`</sub>

**Runs against:** READS Exchange Online and on-premises message tracking. Writes nothing.

Traces a message across BOTH halves of a hybrid tenant in one search.

In hybrid a message crosses two systems that answer different questions, and
answering "where did it go" normally means running two tools with two
vocabularies and stitching the result together by hand. This does that part.

THE TWO SYSTEMS DISAGREE ABOUT WHAT A ROW IS. Exchange Online returns one row
per recipient with a final status. On-premises returns one row per EVENT --
received, then sent, then delivered -- so one message is three or four rows.
This groups them, so a message appears ONCE per recipient with a single
outcome. Double-click it to see every hop in order across both systems.

ON-PREMISES IS THE SLOW HALF because there is no organisation-wide view: each
transport server has to be asked separately. That is why the source starts on
Exchange Online only.

IF A SERVER DOES NOT ANSWER IT SAYS SO -- "3 of 4 servers answered", naming
the one that failed. Rows will be missing when that happens. A trace that
quietly returns less is how somebody concludes a message never existed.

THE TWO 90-DAY BUTTONS ARE NOT THE SAME REPORT, and the difference decides
which question you can answer:

  90 day Enhanced   up to 100,000 rows. Summary fields plus direction and
                    original client IP. Use it for "did this arrive, and
                    where did it go" across a lot of mail.

  90 day Extended   full routing and per-event detail, but capped at 1,000
                    ROWS -- a hundredth of Enhanced. Use it on ONE message or
                    a very narrow search. Pointed at a busy mailbox for 90
                    days it stops at 1,000 and does not say so, and the CSV
                    looks complete when it is not.

Both are emailed as a CSV and neither fills the grid. Both need a sender,
recipient or message ID -- the service refuses without one. Both are Exchange
Online only.

ARCHIVED DATA LAGS LIVE DATA BY 1-4 HOURS, so a message sent this morning may
be missing from a report whose range covers today. Use a normal search for
anything recent.

## Unified Trace

<sub>`Unified-Trace.ps1`</sub>

**Runs against:** Reads Exchange Online and on-premises message traces. Prompts for API credentials on first use. Read-only.

One search across every system a message crosses.

WHAT WORKS TODAY:
  Exchange Online   real, via Get-MessageTraceV2
  On-premises       real, via Get-MessageTrackingLog across the hub servers

WHAT DOES NOT WORK YET:
  Proofpoint        credential prompt works, the API call is not built
  SendGrid          credential prompt works, the API call is not built

THAT IS NOT A BUG AND THE TOOL SAYS SO RATHER THAN RETURNING NOTHING. There
are no API keys yet. When they arrive the credential half is already done and
only the query needs writing.

CREDENTIALS ARE ASKED FOR ONCE PER SESSION, and only for the source you
actually select. They are held in memory and never written to disk. Settings
has a "Forget API credentials" item that clears them.

For a demonstration of the finished view with invented data, use
Unified Trace (Mockup).

## Unified Trace (End User)

<sub>`Unified-Trace-EndUser.ps1`</sub>

**Runs against:** NOTHING. Every row is generated locally. No system is contacted.

Find out what happened to an email.

Type the address the message was sent TO, choose a date range, and press
Trace. You get one line per message showing where it ended up.

WHAT THE RESULT MEANS

  Delivered     It arrived. If the recipient cannot see it, that is almost
                always an inbox rule or the Junk folder rather than anything
                that happened in transit.

  Held          Our email security filter stopped it. It has NOT arrived, and
                the recipient has no way of knowing it exists. The service
                desk can review it and let it through.

  Not sent      We did not send it, usually because the address bounced
                before or was reported as spam. Sending again will not help
                until that is cleared.

  Still going   It has not failed and it is not lost. Something at the
                receiving end asked us to try later and we are still trying.
                Do not send it again -- that usually makes it slower.

  Refused       The receiving side rejected it outright. Whoever sent it
                should have had a bounce message back.

Click the [+] beside a message to see every step it took.

WHAT THIS TOOL CANNOT DO

It cannot read the contents of an email, it cannot release a held message,
and it cannot resend anything. It only tells you where a message got to.
Anything that needs an action goes to the service desk.

THE DATES MATTER. Searching a narrow range around when the message was sent
is both faster and easier to read than searching a week.

## Unified Trace (Mockup)

<sub>`Unified-Trace-Mockup.ps1`</sub>

**Runs against:** NOTHING. Every row is generated locally. No system is contacted.

A MOCKUP of a single message trace spanning every system mail crosses here.

EVERY ROW IS INVENTED. This tool does not connect to Exchange, Proofpoint or
SendGrid -- there is no API access to the last two, which is the whole reason
it exists. It is a working sketch of what a consolidated trace COULD look
like, so the idea can be judged before anybody buys anything.

FIVE SOURCES, and the point is seeing them on one timeline:

  ExO         Exchange Online
  OnPrem      on-premises Exchange transport
  Proofpoint  the primary pod -- inbound filtering
  SER         Proofpoint Secure Email Relay -- application-generated mail
  SendGrid    transactional send, and the suppression lists that silently
              stop it

WHY THIS IS WORTH BUILDING FOR REAL. "They never got the email" is currently
four separate investigations in four consoles, and the answer is usually in
the one you check last. The two SendGrid outcomes below are the clearest
example: a message that was never sent at all because the address is on a
suppression list leaves NO trace in Exchange, so the Exchange-only answer is
"no such message" -- which is true and useless.

THE REMOVE BUTTONS DO NOTHING. They show the confirmation and report what the
real call would have been. They cannot change anything, because there is
nothing connected to change.

Try bob.smith@gcearth.com as a recipient. The mock data rotates through
several scenarios, so searching twice gives a different story each time.
